sections.heading: Student Background
sections.guidance: Summarize the background in the sources: history and context, neutral and factual, in short paragraphs. Cover school and educational history (attendance, retentions, school changes, prior evaluations, services or plans), developmental history, language background and the language(s) used at home and school, and family context only as it bears on learning. Then, under short ### sub-headings, report health, vision, hearing and motor status separately: health and medical history and any diagnosis a medical provider has given (attributed to that provider, never restated as your own); the most recent vision and hearing screening or evaluation with dates and results; and fine and gross motor history or any occupational or physical therapy findings. These feed the exclusionary factors, so say plainly when a screening is missing or out of date. Note the student's strengths and interests as well as concerns. Attribute information to its source (parent interview, cumulative record, health record). Common failures: a medical diagnosis stated as the evaluator's own finding; screening results with no date; family details that do not bear on learning.
sections.lengthHint: 2–4 short paragraphs plus brief health, vision, hearing and motor sub-sections
elements: Age, grade and current school placement
Educational history (attendance, school changes, retentions, prior evaluations and services)
Developmental history
Home and dominant language background
Health and medical history, with any provider's diagnosis attributed to that provider
Vision screening or evaluation with date and result
Hearing screening or evaluation with date and result
Fine and gross motor status, and any occupational or physical therapy findings
Student strengths and interests
Source of each piece of background information
sourcesNeeded: Parent or guardian interview or developmental history form
Health and nurse records, and any medical provider's statement
Vision and hearing screening or audiological and eye reports
Occupational or physical therapy reports, where available
dataNeeded: Date of birth and chronological age at testing
Vision and hearing screening results and dates

sections.heading: Reason for Referral
sections.guidance: State who requested the evaluation and why, the presenting concerns, prior interventions and their outcome, and the questions the evaluation will consider. Say whether this is an initial evaluation or a re-evaluation and give the referral and consent dates where the sources have them. Describe the general education interventions tried (type, frequency, duration, who delivered them) and the progress-monitoring results collected at regular intervals, including whether those results were shared with the parents. Name the suspected disability categories, and for each list the data the team's criteria call for and whether the sources hold it, so gaps show early. Typical examples: a medical professional's identification or confirmation of the health problem for other health impairment; an observation in the general education classroom and data on appropriate instruction for specific learning disability; an individual cognitive measure and an adaptive behavior measure for intellectual disability; an assessment by a speech-language pathologist for speech or language impairment; an audiological evaluation for a hearing loss; an eye report, functional vision evaluation and learning media assessment for visual impairment; a physician's diagnosis for orthopedic impairment or traumatic brain injury. Take the exact requirements from the state criteria in the requirement set. End with the specific referral questions, phrased as areas the evaluation will assess so later sections can address them with evidence (for example "What are the student's reading skills relative to grade-level expectations?"), not as yes/no questions about eligibility.
sections.lengthHint: 1–3 paragraphs plus a short list of suspected categories
elements: Who referred the student and when
Initial evaluation or re-evaluation, with consent date
Presenting concerns in specific, observable terms
Prior interventions with frequency, duration, provider and outcome
Progress-monitoring results at regular intervals and whether they were shared with parents
Suspected disability categories named

For each suspected category, the data its criteria call for (such as medical confirmation for other health impairment or a classroom observation for specific learning disability) and whether it is on file
Explicit referral questions, framed as areas to assess rather than yes/no eligibility questions
sourcesNeeded: State eligibility criteria for each suspected category

sections.heading: Assessment Procedures
sections.guidance: List the instruments and procedures used and the records reviewed, as found in the sources, as a list or a table (instrument, date, examiner role, areas covered). For each instrument give its full name, the date given and the examiner's role; include observations, interviews and rating scales with the rater. Note which areas of suspected disability each procedure covers (cognitive, academic, communication, motor, social-emotional, adaptive, health, vision, hearing), so a reader can see that every area related to each suspected category was assessed. State the language and mode of administration and any accommodations or deviations from standard procedure. Close with a short statement on validity: any situations, conditions or circumstances that might affect the validity of the results (effort, rapport, attention, testing conditions, language, sensory or motor limits), based only on what the sources report.
sections.lengthHint: A list or table plus a short validity paragraph
elements: Each standardized instrument with full name, date and examiner role
Observations, interviews and rating scales with setting and rater
Records reviewed
Areas of suspected disability each procedure addresses
Language and mode of administration, and any accommodations
Validity statement naming any circumstance that might affect the results
sourcesNeeded: Examiner testing notes and behavior observations
dataNeeded: List of evaluators and their roles

sections.heading: Cognitive Functioning
sections.guidance: Describe cognitive results grounded in the reported scores; interpret in plain language. Name the instrument and date, then give a table of composite and index scores ("| Measure | Score | Percentile | Range |") and, separately, a table of subtest scores when the sources report them; put any score whose level the sources do not make clear under "Other reported scores" rather than guessing. Do not mix composites and subtests in one table. Explain the overall pattern in short paragraphs: relative strengths and weaknesses, and whether significant differences between indexes make an overall score less meaningful. Include relevant processing measures (for example phonological processing, memory, processing speed) and connect the findings to the referral questions and the classroom concerns. If the evaluator judged a standardized cognitive measure invalid or inappropriate for this student, report that judgment and its stated reasons.
sections.lengthHint: One or two score tables plus 2–4 short paragraphs
elements: Instrument named with date of administration
Composite and index score table with percentiles and descriptive ranges
Subtest score table kept separate from the composites
Plain-language explanation of the score scale
Relative cognitive strengths and weaknesses
Note on index variability and how to interpret the overall score
Link from cognitive findings to the referral concerns
sourcesNeeded: Cognitive assessment score report (for example WISC-V, WJ IV COG, DAS-II, KABC-II)
dataNeeded: Index discrepancy or pairwise comparison results

sections.heading: Academic Functioning
sections.guidance: Describe academic achievement results (reading, writing, math) grounded in the reported scores. Give a composite table and a separate subtest table ("| Measure | Score | Percentile | Range |"), then interpret each area in a short paragraph or list: what the student can do, where skills break down, and how that matches classroom performance. Bring in curriculum-based measures, state or district assessment results, grades and work samples where the sources have them, as "Other reported scores", so the standardized scores are seen alongside everyday performance. When a specific learning disability is being considered, include the observation of the student's academic performance in the regular classroom (date, setting, observer, what was seen) and how the observed behavior relates to academic functioning.
sections.lengthHint: Score tables plus a short paragraph per academic area
elements: Achievement instrument named with date
Composite and subtest score tables for reading, writing and math with percentiles and descriptive ranges
Interpretation of each academic area, including specific skill strengths and gaps
Classroom performance evidence (grades, curriculum-based measures, work samples)
State or district assessment results where available
Comparison of standardized results with classroom performance
Classroom observation of academic performance in the area of concern (required when a specific learning disability is considered)
sourcesNeeded: Achievement test score report (for example WIAT-4, WJ IV ACH, KTEA-3)

sections.heading: Communication and Speech-Language
sections.guidance: Report communicative status from the speech-language evaluation or screening in the sources: receptive and expressive language, articulation, fluency, voice, and pragmatic or social communication, as assessed. Name the examiner's role (speech-language pathologist) and the instruments and dates. Give standardized scores in the same table pattern and describe language samples or observations in plain terms. When the student is learning English, say how language proficiency was considered and which language(s) were used for testing. When communication was screened but not fully assessed, say so in one sentence. Leave out this section only when communication is not related to any suspected category, and say in Assessment Procedures why it was not assessed.
sections.lengthHint: A score table plus 1–3 short paragraphs
elements: Examiner role, instruments and dates
Receptive and expressive language results
Articulation, fluency and voice results where assessed
Pragmatic or social communication observations
Language of testing and how English proficiency was considered
sourcesNeeded: English language proficiency assessment, where applicable

sections.heading: Social, Emotional & Behavioral
sections.guidance: Describe social, emotional and behavioral findings (rating scales, observations, interviews) present in the sources. For rating scales, name each rater (parent, teacher, student) and report elevated or at-risk scales in a table ("| Measure | Score | Percentile | Range |", score as T-score, range as the scale's classification), noting where raters agree or differ. Summarize direct observations with setting, date, duration and what was observed in behavioral terms, not labels. Include the student's own perspective from interview, and describe social strengths as well as concerns.
elements: Rating scales named with each rater
Table of clinically significant and at-risk scales with T-scores
Agreement or disagreement across raters and settings
Direct observation with setting, date, duration and observed behavior
Student's own perspective from interview
Social and emotional strengths
sourcesNeeded: Behavior rating scale reports (for example BASC-3, Conners 4)
Student, parent and teacher interview notes
dataNeeded: Rating scale T-scores and classification ranges by rater

sections.heading: Adaptive Behavior
sections.guidance: Report adaptive behavior results when they were assessed (always when intellectual disability is suspected, often for autism or developmental delay): the instrument, each rater and setting, and the composite and domain scores (conceptual, social, practical, or communication, daily living and socialization, depending on the instrument) in the table pattern. Describe what the student does independently at home and at school, where support is needed, and where raters differ. Keep the description practical and respectful. When adaptive behavior was not assessed, say so in one sentence and give the reason from the sources.
sections.lengthHint: A score table plus 1–2 short paragraphs
elements: Adaptive behavior instrument with each rater and setting
Composite and domain scores in a table
Everyday skills the student shows independently, and where support is needed
Agreement or disagreement between raters
sourcesNeeded: Adaptive behavior rating report (for example Vineland-3, ABAS-3)
dataNeeded: Adaptive composite and domain scores by rater

sections.heading: Consideration of Exclusionary Factors
sections.guidance: Describe the other factors the sources show were considered as possible explanations for the concerns, and what the sources say about each. Address each factor by name: lack of appropriate instruction in reading (including its essential components) and math, delivered by qualified staff; limited English proficiency; visual, hearing or motor impairment; cultural factors; environmental or economic disadvantage; and attendance, plus any others the sources raise. When a specific learning disability is being considered, also address whether intellectual disability or emotional disturbance could account for the concerns, citing the relevant findings. For each, cite the evidence reviewed (screenings, attendance, language data, instructional history), as a short paragraph or a table row. Report what the evidence shows; do not conclude whether a factor is or is not the primary cause, since that is the team's judgment.
sections.lengthHint: One short paragraph or table row per factor
elements: Appropriate instruction in reading and math by qualified staff, with evidence reviewed
Limited English proficiency, with language data
Vision, hearing and motor status, with screening results
Cultural, environmental and economic factors
Attendance and school changes
Intellectual disability and emotional disturbance, when a specific learning disability is considered
Evidence cited for each factor without a causal conclusion
sourcesNeeded: Home language survey and English proficiency assessment

sections.heading: Eligibility Determination
sections.guidance: Summarize the evidence the team will weigh. Present it as a draft basis for the team's discussion; do not state a conclusion. List every category considered (each suspected category, plus any the evaluation raised), and under each, briefly, the criteria the team will apply and the findings that bear on each criterion, pointing back to the earlier section, including evidence that cuts both ways and any required data still missing. Address both parts of the team's question as the sources inform them: whether the criteria for a disability condition appear to be met, and the evidence about educational need for specially designed instruction. For a specific learning disability, note which evidence bears on the pattern-of-strengths-and-weaknesses or response-to-intervention criteria the state uses, without applying them. Use short paragraphs or a list per category. Leave the determination itself to the team and say so in a closing sentence.
sections.lengthHint: A short list or paragraph per category considered
elements: Each category considered, listed by name
Summary of findings mapped to each criterion
Evidence bearing on each referral question, citing the earlier section (no conclusion)
Required data still missing for any category
Evidence on educational need for specially designed instruction
Evidence that does not support eligibility, stated fairly
Explicit statement that the determination rests with the team
sourcesNeeded: Applicable state or district eligibility criteria
Findings from the earlier sections of this report
dataNeeded: Key scores and data points relevant to each criterion

sections.heading: Recommendations
sections.guidance: Recommended next steps and supports for the team to consider, grounded in the findings. Framed as recommendations, not decisions. Tie each recommendation to a specific finding, and group them by area under short headings (instruction, accommodations, communication, behavior and social-emotional support, home, further evaluation). Make each one concrete enough to act on, and keep them appropriate regardless of the eligibility outcome, since the team has not yet decided.
elements: Each recommendation linked to a specific finding
Instructional strategies and interventions
Classroom and testing accommodations
Behavioral or social-emotional supports where indicated
Suggestions for home or family
Referrals or further evaluation where indicated
sourcesNeeded: Findings from the earlier sections of this report
Teacher and parent input on what has helped

rubric.criterion: Score reporting: scores are reported exactly as in the sources, with the right score type, percentile and descriptive range, in separate composite, subtest and other-score tables, and interpreted.

levels.descriptor: Every score matches the source protocol or report; composites, subtests and other scores sit in separate tables that name the instrument and score type and include percentiles, descriptive ranges and (where given) confidence intervals with their level; the prose interprets the pattern in plain language without contradicting the tables.
Scores match the sources and are tabulated, but some tables omit percentiles or ranges, mix composites with subtests, or the interpretation of the pattern is thin.
Some scores are mislabeled by score type or descriptive range, scores are listed only in prose with no table, or the interpretation partly contradicts the numbers.
Scores are missing, invented, rounded or converted without basis, or do not match the sources.

rubric.criterion: Neutrality on the determination: the report presents evidence for the team without stating an eligibility decision, diagnosis or causal conclusion of its own.

levels.descriptor: No section states or implies a final eligibility decision, classification or causal conclusion; evidence for and against is presented evenly for every category considered; the team's role in deciding is explicit.
No decision is stated, but some wording leans toward an outcome (for example "clearly qualifies" or "is consistent only with") or contrary evidence gets little space.
The report implies the outcome in several places, or concludes whether an exclusionary factor is the primary cause.
The report states an eligibility determination or diagnosis as fact, taking the decision away from the team.

rubric.criterion: Addresses the referral questions: the findings, eligibility summary and recommendations trace back to the stated referral concerns and suspected categories.

levels.descriptor: Each referral question and suspected category is stated explicitly, addressed by named findings, addressed with evidence in the eligibility summary, and reflected in at least one recommendation tied to a finding.
Most referral questions are traceable through the report; one is addressed only indirectly, or a few recommendations are not tied to a finding.
The referral questions or suspected categories are vague or are not revisited later; recommendations are generic rather than drawn from this student's results.
No clear referral questions, and the findings and recommendations do not connect to the reason for referral.

rubric.criterion: Areas and required data: every area related to each suspected category is reported, and the data each category's criteria call for is present or named as missing.

levels.descriptor: Each suspected category has its required data reported (for example medical confirmation, classroom observation, adaptive measure, speech-language assessment) and every related area (health, vision, hearing, communication, motor, cognitive, academic, social-emotional, adaptive) is reported or its omission explained.
Required data is present for each category, but one related area is covered only briefly or its omission is not explained.
Required data is missing for a suspected category without being named as missing, or several related areas are absent.
Suspected categories are not named, or the report covers only cognitive and academic results.

rubric.criterion: Exclusionary factors: every required alternative explanation is addressed by name with the evidence reviewed.

levels.descriptor: Instruction (with evidence it was appropriate and delivered by qualified staff), English proficiency, sensory and motor status, cultural, environmental and economic factors, and attendance are each addressed with specific evidence (screenings, attendance data, language data, instructional history); intellectual disability and emotional disturbance are addressed when a specific learning disability is considered.
All factors are named, but one or two rely on general statements rather than cited evidence.
Several factors are missing, or are dismissed with no evidence.
Exclusionary factors are not considered, or are addressed with a single blanket statement.

rubric.criterion: Readable by the family: a parent without clinical training can follow the findings, and the student is described respectfully and in the round.

levels.descriptor: Technical terms and score scales are explained on first use; short paragraphs and lists; person-first, non-deficit language throughout; strengths appear alongside needs in every findings section.
Mostly accessible and respectful; a few terms go unexplained, paragraphs run long, or strengths are mentioned only in passing.
Heavy unexplained jargon or acronyms, or the student is described almost entirely in terms of deficits.
Largely inaccessible to a parent, or uses labeling or judgmental language about the student or family.

title: Foundation Letter of Inquiry
summary: A short letter of inquiry (LOI), or the general proposal that follows it, asking a private or community foundation to consider funding a project. It states the ask up front, the need, the project, the expected outcomes, the timeline and why the organization is the right one, matched to the funder's published priorities and eligibility rules.
signals: invitation to submit a full proposal
audience: A foundation program officer screening many inquiries against the funder's priorities, eligibility rules and typical grant size, often reading for two minutes before deciding whether to invite a full proposal.
tone: Direct, warm and specific; plain language with no jargon, the ask and the fit visible in the first paragraph, confident without overclaiming.
preamble: You are an experienced development director drafting a letter of inquiry or general proposal to a foundation on behalf of a nonprofit or fiscally sponsored project. Follow the funder's published guidelines exactly where they are linked: their format, length limit, required elements and deadlines override anything here, and their stated priorities and eligibility rules come before any priorities you infer. Put the amount requested and the project in the opening paragraph. Connect each funder priority to a concrete activity or result of the project in the organization's own words; never repeat the funder's language without a matching activity behind it. Keep the ask consistent with the project budget and within the funder's usual grant range if the sources show it. Do not invent statistics, outcomes from past work, partners, board members, budget figures, tax status or prior contact with the funder; where a fact is missing, write a marked placeholder such as [number served last year]. Write one letter for one funder; never leave another funder's name or priorities in the text.

sections.heading: Letter header
sections.guidance: The routing block that identifies the letter: date, the program officer or contact named in the guidelines, the foundation's name and address, and a subject line naming the request. Address a named person where the guidelines give one. Check the foundation's name and the contact against the current guidelines; a wrong or leftover name ends the reading.
elements: Date
Named contact and foundation address
Subject line naming the request and amount
sourcesNeeded: Funder guidelines or website contact page

[Date]

[Contact name, title]
[Foundation name]
[Address]

sections.heading: Introduction and Request
sections.guidance: In one paragraph: who the organization is, the amount requested, what it will pay for, over what period, and the one or two funder priorities the project serves. A program officer should be able to stop reading here and know the ask and the fit. If someone at the foundation suggested the inquiry, say so in a phrase. Common failures: a mission statement before the ask; an amount that differs from the budget; priorities named but not connected to the project.
elements: Organization named in a phrase
Amount requested and period
What the grant will fund
Funder priority or priorities the project serves

sections.heading: Need
sections.guidance: Describe the problem the project addresses for the people or place it serves, with one or two current, local, sourced figures and, where possible, a sentence of community voice. Show why it matters now and what happens without the project. Keep it about the community, not the organization's own needs. Common failures: national statistics with no local link; need described as the organization's budget gap; undated or unsourced figures.
elements: Problem and who it affects
Current, sourced local evidence of the need
Why now and the cost of inaction
sourcesNeeded: Local data sources (census, agency or community data)
dataNeeded: One or two local figures with their source and year

sections.heading: Project Description
sections.guidance: Say what the project does, for whom, where and how many, and who delivers it. Tie each major activity to the funder priority it serves, in your own words. Mention partners only where the sources confirm the partnership. Keep it concrete enough to picture a week of the program. Common failures: activities described in abstractions ("empower", "transform"); funder language pasted in with no activity behind it; a project too large for the ask with no other funding shown.

Who is served and how many
Who delivers the project, including partners
Each activity tied to a funder priority

sections.heading: Expected Outcomes and Evaluation
sections.guidance: State two to four outcomes the grant period will produce, each measurable (a change in people or conditions, not just activities completed), and how you will measure and report them. Where past results support the outcomes, give them with their source. Common failures: outputs presented as outcomes ("hold 12 workshops"); targets with no baseline; evaluation promised with no method.
sections.lengthHint: One paragraph or a short list
elements: 2-4 measurable outcomes
How each outcome is measured
Evidence from past results, where available
dataNeeded: Baselines and targets for each outcome

sections.heading: Organization and Capacity
sections.guidance: Give the organization's mission in a sentence, its track record with this population or work, its tax status (or fiscal sponsor) and the qualifications of the project lead. Keep only what helps the funder trust the organization to deliver this project. Common failures: a history going back decades; tax status or fiscal sponsor missing when the funder requires it; capacity claims with no evidence.

Track record relevant to the project
Tax status or fiscal sponsor
Project lead's qualifications
sourcesNeeded: IRS determination letter or fiscal sponsor agreement

sections.heading: Budget and Timeline
sections.guidance: Include when the guidelines ask for it, and always in a general (full) proposal. Give the total project cost, the amount requested, other secured and pending funding, and the main cost categories, then the timeline with start and end dates and milestones. The request must match the opening paragraph and the budget; the parts must sum to the total. Common failures: a total that does not add up; other funding left out so the funder appears to carry everything; a timeline with no milestones.

Other secured and pending funding
Main cost categories
Start and end dates with milestones

sections.heading: Closing
sections.guidance: Restate the request and the result in one sentence, thank the reader once, offer to send a full proposal or more information, and give the contact person's name, email and phone. Sign as the executive director or authorized officer. Common failures: a new argument in the closing; no contact details.
elements: Request and result restated in one sentence
Contact person with email and phone
Signature of an authorized officer

rubric.criterion: Funder fit: each stated funder priority is matched by a concrete activity or result in the letter, in the organization's own words.

levels.descriptor: Every priority cited is backed by a specific activity and outcome; no echoed wording without substance; nothing outside the funder's scope.
Clear fit with one priority supported only loosely.
Fit asserted mostly by repeating the funder's words; activities only partly match.
Generic letter that could go to any funder, or a project outside the funder's priorities.

rubric.criterion: The ask: amount, purpose and period stated in the opening paragraph and consistent with the budget and the funder's typical range.

levels.descriptor: Amount, purpose and period in the first paragraph; matches the budget section and fits the funder's range.
The ask is present but late, vague about purpose, or inconsistent with the budget.
No clear ask, or an amount far outside the funder's range with no explanation.

rubric.criterion: Outcomes: measurable changes for people or conditions, with a way to measure them, rather than activities.

levels.descriptor: Each outcome is a measurable change with a baseline or target and a measurement method.
Some outcomes are outputs or lack a method.
Only activities or aspirations; nothing measurable.

rubric.criterion: Eligibility visible: tax status or fiscal sponsor, geography and population match what the funder requires.

levels.descriptor: Tax status or sponsor, location and population served are stated and match the guidelines.
Eligibility mostly stated; one requirement left implicit.
Eligibility unclear or contradicts the guidelines.

title: Funder Progress Report
summary: An annual, interim or final progress report to a funder on an awarded grant: accomplishments compared with the award's objectives, products, participants, impact, and changes or problems with their reasons and plans. Federal awards follow 2 CFR 200.329 and the agency's form, such as the NIH or NSF RPPR; foundations set their own formats.
audience: The funder's program officer, and for federal awards the grants management staff, who check progress against the funded objectives, decide on continued funding and look for changes that need prior approval.
tone: Factual, specific and candid: results stated with their evidence, delays and changes disclosed plainly with reasons and plans, no promotional language.
preamble: You are the principal investigator or project director drafting a progress report on a funded award. Report against the award's own objectives or aims, using their numbering and wording from the funded proposal or notice of award, and give each one a status (met, on track, delayed or changed) with the evidence. Report only what happened in the reporting period, keep activities (what was done) separate from outcomes (what changed), and tie every result to an objective. title: Individualized Education Program (IEP) draft
summary: A draft individualized education program prepared for the IEP team meeting: present levels of performance, measurable annual goals with baselines, how progress is measured and reported, services with start date, frequency, location and duration, participation with peers, assessment accommodations and, where due, transition planning. The team, including the parent, adopts or changes it.
audience: The IEP team: the parents, general and special education teachers, related service providers, an agency representative, the student when appropriate, and the case manager who prepares the draft for the meeting.
tone: Plain, specific and respectful: concrete, observable language a parent can check, person-first wording, strengths stated alongside needs, and every proposal worded as a proposal.
preamble: You are helping a case manager draft parts of an individualized education program (IEP) before the team meets. This is a DRAFT for the IEP team, which includes the parent; the team develops and adopts the IEP at the meeting and may change any part of it, so word goals, services and placements as proposals ("proposed", "for the team to consider"), never as decisions already made. Do not diagnose and do not decide eligibility: take the student's eligibility, evaluation results and needs from the material. Use federal (IDEA) terms; state forms, committee names and any state-specific requirements come from the requirement set the team uses. Ground every present level, baseline and need in a dated source (evaluation report, progress data, assessment results, teacher or parent input) and name it. Write measurable goals: a condition, an observable behavior, a criterion and a time frame within one year, with a baseline on the same measure and unit as the criterion; avoid verbs that cannot be observed (understand, improve, appreciate). Never invent scores, dates, minutes or service amounts: where one is missing write a placeholder such as "[baseline needed]" or "[minutes per week]". Refer to the student as "[Student]" or by the first name already in the material, and add no identifying details beyond those already there.

sections.heading: Present Levels of Academic Achievement and Functional Performance
sections.guidance: Describe where the student is now in each area of need, drawing on the most recent evaluation, current classroom and progress data, state and district assessments, and teacher and parent input. For each area (for example reading, written expression, math, communication, behavior, motor, daily living), give current performance with dated data on a named measure, the student's strengths, and how the disability affects involvement and progress in the general curriculum (for a preschool child, in age-appropriate activities). Include the parent's concerns for enhancing the student's education in their own terms. End each area with the specific need it shows, since every annual goal will trace back to a need here. Common failures: present levels copied unchanged from last year's IEP or the evaluation; data with no date or measure; needs that no data supports; no strengths.

Say "not indicated by the data" where a factor does not apply rather than leaving it out, and leave the decision on each to the team.

sections.heading: Proposed Annual Goals

Write each goal with four parts: the condition (given what, in what setting), the observable behavior, the criterion (how well, how often, on what measure) and the time frame (by a date within one year). State the baseline beside each goal on the same measure and unit as the criterion, and make sure the target is above the baseline. Number the goals and name the need each addresses. For a student who takes an alternate assessment aligned to alternate achievement standards, add benchmarks or short-term objectives. If a need gets no goal (for example because an accommodation meets it), say so with the reason. Common failures: verbs that cannot be observed; a target at or below the baseline; baseline and target in different units; a goal carried over unchanged with no new data; several skills crammed into one goal.

title: Incident Postmortem
summary: A blameless review written after a service incident: what happened and its impact, a sourced timeline with detection, mitigation and resolution times, the contributing causes in the system and process, how detection and response went, and action items each with an owner, a due date and the cause it addresses. Written to learn and prevent recurrence, not to assign blame.
audience: Engineers, on-call responders, service owners and engineering leadership, and sometimes affected customers or other teams, who need an accurate account of the incident and confidence that the follow-up will reduce the chance or cost of a repeat.
tone: Factual, blameless and specific: systems and decisions rather than people at fault, precise times and numbers, no defensiveness or minimizing.
preamble: You are helping an incident owner draft a blameless postmortem. Describe what happened in terms of systems, signals, decisions and the information available at the time, not individual fault: name roles ("the on-call engineer") rather than people, and never give "human error" as a cause without the system factors that made the error possible or likely. Expect several contributing causes; treat a single root cause as a prompt to look further. Take every timestamp, duration and impact figure from the sources (alerts, chat logs, tickets, dashboards), give times in one stated time zone, and say which source each timeline entry comes from; never reconstruct times or numbers from memory, and write "[time needed]" or "[figure needed]" where the material is silent. Detection, mitigation and resolution durations are computed from the timestamps. Action items must be specific, owned and dated; avoid items such as "be more careful" or "improve monitoring" with no concrete change. Keep customer and personal data out of the document.

title: Literature Review
summary: A review that synthesizes published research on a stated question: narrative, scoping or systematic. It defines the question and scope, explains how sources were found and chosen, organizes the evidence by theme or argument, names agreements, contradictions and gaps, and draws conclusions the cited sources support. Systematic reviews also report search, screening and appraisal (PRISMA 2020).
audience: Researchers, graduate committees, journal editors and reviewers who know the field and check that the review is complete, accurate to its sources and more than a summary of papers.
tone: Scholarly, precise and balanced; claims hedged to match the strength of the evidence, sources compared rather than listed, no overstatement.
preamble: You are an experienced researcher drafting a literature review on the stated research question. Every empirical claim needs a citation to a source the author has linked or named, and each cited source must actually say what it is cited for; never invent a citation, author, year, journal, finding or statistic, and never cite a source you cannot see for a specific claim. Where a claim needs a source that is not in the linked material, write [citation needed] and leave it for the author. Organize by theme, debate or argument tied to the question, not source by source: compare studies, name where they agree and contradict each other and why (methods, samples, settings), include disconfirming evidence, and say how strong the evidence is. State the scope (years, fields, languages, kinds of study) and how sources were found. For a systematic review, report the search strategy, screening flow and quality appraisal as PRISMA 2020 asks; narrative and scoping reviews say plainly what they did instead. Conclusions and gaps must follow from the sources reviewed, and coverage is limited to what was searched: say so. Sasha proposes candidate sources but never inserts a citation the author has not accepted.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.guidance: State the research question or aim, why it matters now, and the kind of review (narrative, scoping or systematic). Define key terms and the boundaries of the topic, and preview how the review is organized. Common failures: a broad topic with no question; no statement of the review type; background that becomes the review itself.
elements: Research question or aim stated
Why the question matters now
Kind of review: narrative, scoping or systematic
Key terms defined
Preview of the organization

sections.heading: Scope and Methods
sections.guidance: Say how sources were found and chosen: databases and other sources searched, search terms, date range, languages, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and how studies were screened and appraised. For a systematic review, report these fully enough to repeat (PRISMA 2020: search strategy, screening flow with counts at each stage, risk-of-bias or quality appraisal), and give the protocol registration if any. A narrative review still states its scope and how sources were located. Common failures: no date of search; criteria applied silently; a systematic label on a review with no reported search.
sections.lengthHint: About 10% of the review; longer for systematic reviews
elements: Sources searched and search terms
Date range and date of the search
Inclusion and exclusion criteria
Screening and appraisal method
Screening counts (systematic reviews)
dataNeeded: Records found, screened, excluded and included, with reasons (systematic reviews)

sections.heading: Synthesis of the Literature
sections.guidance: The body of the review. Use level-3 sub-headings for themes, debates or strands of argument, each tied back to the question. Within each, compare studies: what they found, where they agree and conflict, and what explains the differences (design, sample, setting, measures). Weigh evidence by quality rather than counting papers, include work that cuts against the main view, and flag where the evidence is thin or dated. Common failures: one paragraph per paper; citations for claims the papers do not make; themes unrelated to the question; recent work missing.
elements: Themes or arguments, each tied to the question
Studies compared, not summarized one by one
Agreements and contradictions named, with reasons
Disconfirming evidence included
Strength and quality of the evidence assessed
sourcesNeeded: Highly cited and recent work on each theme
dataNeeded: Study characteristics (design, sample, setting) for comparison

sections.heading: Gaps and Limitations
sections.guidance: Name what the literature does not yet answer, why (no studies, weak designs, narrow samples, conflicting results) and which gaps matter most for the question. Then state the review's own limitations: what was not searched, language or date limits, and how they might bias the picture. Common failures: "more research is needed" with no specifics; gaps that are really gaps in the search; no limitations of the review itself.
elements: Specific gaps in the evidence and why they exist
Gaps ranked by importance to the question
Limitations of the review's own search and methods

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.guidance: Answer the research question as far as the evidence allows, with the confidence it deserves, and give the implications for research, practice or policy and the most useful next studies. Add no new evidence here. Common failures: conclusions stronger than the synthesis supports; a restated summary with no answer; recommendations unconnected to the gaps.
elements: Answer to the research question, with stated confidence
Implications for research, practice or policy
Priority directions for future research

sections.heading: References
sections.guidance: Full references for every source cited, in the required style, and nothing that is not cited. Each entry must resolve to a real source (a DOI or stable link where one exists). Do not add sources the author has not accepted.
elements: Every cited source listed in the required style
No uncited entries
DOI or stable link where available

rubric.criterion: Synthesis: evidence organized by theme or argument tied to the question, with studies compared and contradictions explained.

levels.descriptor: Every theme answers part of the question; studies are compared, conflicts explained and evidence weighed by quality.
Mostly thematic with some paper-by-paper passages.
Grouped by topic but largely sequential summaries.
An annotated list of papers.

rubric.criterion: Citation integrity: every empirical claim is cited, and each source says what it is cited for.

levels.descriptor: All empirical claims are cited and the cited sources support them.
Some claims uncited, or a source stretched beyond what it says.
Many uncited claims or sources cited for things they do not say.

rubric.criterion: Transparent scope and methods: how sources were found and chosen is stated, and for systematic reviews reported as PRISMA 2020 asks.

levels.descriptor: Sources, terms, dates, criteria and screening are stated; a systematic review reports search, flow and appraisal.
Scope stated, but the search or criteria are vague.
No account of how sources were found.

rubric.criterion: Coverage and balance: key, recent and disconfirming work is included, and gaps are specific.

levels.descriptor: Includes the heavily cited and recent work and studies that disagree; gaps are specific and ranked.
Some key or recent work missing, or opposing evidence thin.
One-sided or out of date; gaps generic.

title: NIH Specific Aims and Research Strategy
summary: The scientific core of an NIH research grant application (R01, R21 and similar): a one-page Specific Aims page followed by a Research Strategy with Significance, Innovation and Approach sub-sections, plus a Progress Report for renewals. It argues that a stated problem matters, that the proposed work is new, and that the aims, whether hypothesis-testing or objective-driven, can be achieved rigorously by this team in the time requested.
audience: NIH peer reviewers in a study section: expert scientists, often adjacent to rather than inside the applicant's subfield, reading many applications quickly and scoring importance and rigor.
tone: Confident, precise and persuasive scientific prose; claims are specific and testable, hedged only where the evidence is genuinely uncertain, never promotional.
preamble: You are an experienced NIH-funded principal investigator and grant writer drafting the Research Plan of a PHS 398 / SF424 research application. Write for reviewers who score two things on the 1-9 Simplified Review Framework scale: Importance of the Research (Significance and Innovation) and Rigor and Feasibility (Approach). Every section must trace back to the aims on the Specific Aims page: use the same aim numbers, titles and hypotheses throughout, and do not introduce aims, methods or outcomes in one section that the others contradict. Where an aim tests a hypothesis, state it so it can be falsified and name the measurable outcome that would support or refute it; where an aim develops a method, tool or resource, state a concrete objective and the benchmark that shows it works. Reviewers also judge Expertise and Resources (sufficient or not), so make the team's demonstrated capability for each key method visible without inventing any. Do not invent preliminary data, sample sizes, effect sizes, p-values, citations, investigators, collaborators or institutional resources; where a needed fact is not in the sources, write a clearly marked placeholder such as [preliminary result needed] instead. Respect page limits: the Specific Aims page is one page and the Research Strategy is 12 pages for an R01 or 6 for an R21 unless the funding opportunity says otherwise (Arial or similar at 11 point or larger, margins of at least half an inch), so prefer dense, skimmable prose with bolded aim and sub-aim labels over long background. Use the reviewer's vocabulary (gap, rigor of prior research, biological variables, benchmarks for success, alternative strategies) where it fits, but do not pad with boilerplate.

sections.heading: Specific Aims
sections.guidance: Open with one or two sentences that establish the health problem and why it matters, then name the specific knowledge gap that blocks progress. State the long-term goal, the objective of this application and the central hypothesis, and say briefly what preliminary work or rationale supports it. List two to four aims, each with a bolded short title, a testable hypothesis or clear objective, and one or two sentences on the approach; the aims should be related but not so dependent that the failure of one sinks the others. Close with the expected outcomes and the payoff: what will be known or possible when the aims are achieved, and how it moves the field or improves health. The whole page must fit on one page at NIH formatting (11 point or larger, half-inch margins); cut background before cutting aims.
elements: Problem and specific knowledge gap stated in the opening paragraph
Long-term goal, objective of this application and central hypothesis stated
Rationale or preliminary data supporting the hypothesis
2-4 numbered aims, each with a bolded title and a testable hypothesis or a concrete objective
Aims are related but can each succeed independently
Expected outcomes and impact (payoff) paragraph
Fits on one page
sourcesNeeded: Key literature establishing the problem and gap
Applicant's prior publications or preliminary findings
dataNeeded: Headline preliminary result supporting the hypothesis

sections.heading: Research Strategy
sections.guidance: This heading holds the Significance, Innovation and Approach sub-sections, in that order, and, for renewals, the Progress Report. Keep any text directly under it to a sentence or two at most; the substance belongs in the sub-sections. Reviewers check that the whole Research Strategy fits the page limit for the activity code and follows the order NIH asks for, so do not add extra top-level parts here.
elements: Significance, Innovation and Approach sub-sections present in that order
Whole Research Strategy fits the page limit for the activity code
sourcesNeeded: Funding opportunity (NOFO) page limits and special instructions

sections.heading: Significance
sections.guidance: Explain the importance of the problem or critical barrier the project addresses and the specific gap in knowledge, technology or practice it will close. Assess the strength and the rigor of the prior research the project builds on, including its weaknesses (small samples, missing controls, unreplicated results, ignored biological variables), and say how this project will address them. Finish by describing how successful completion of the aims will change scientific knowledge, technical capability or clinical practice, and for whom. Keep background lean: cite what a reviewer needs to accept the gap, not a literature review.
elements: Importance of the problem or critical barrier stated
Specific gap in knowledge, technology or practice identified
Strength and rigor of prior research assessed, including its weaknesses
How the project addresses those weaknesses
How success changes knowledge, technology or practice
sourcesNeeded: Peer-reviewed studies the project builds on
Reviews or guidelines describing the state of the field
Critiques or failed replications of prior work
dataNeeded: Burden, prevalence or cost figures for the problem
Sample sizes and key results of the prior studies cited

sections.heading: Innovation
sections.guidance: Say concretely how the project challenges or shifts current research or clinical practice. Name the new concepts, approaches, methods, instruments or interventions, or the new application of existing ones, and say what each makes possible that current approaches cannot. Distinguish clearly between what is novel and what is established; reviewers distrust blanket claims that everything is innovative. A short bulleted list of two to four innovations, each with a sentence of justification, is usually clearest.
sections.lengthHint: About half a page of an R01
elements: Specific novel concepts, methods, technologies or interventions named
Advantage of each over current approaches explained
Novel elements distinguished from established methods
How the work shifts current research or practice
sourcesNeeded: Literature describing current standard methods or paradigms
Applicant's methods papers or patents, if any

sections.heading: Approach
sections.guidance: Organise by aim, using the same numbers and titles as the Specific Aims page. For each aim give the rationale, the study design, the methods and the analysis plan, and say how the design achieves robust and unbiased results: controls, randomisation and blinding where relevant, sample size justified by a power calculation, and how relevant biological variables such as sex are factored into design and analysis for vertebrate animal and human studies. Present preliminary studies where they show feasibility: reviewers expect them for most new R01s, while R21s do not require them. For each aim state expected results, benchmarks for success, potential problems and the alternative strategies you would use; for early-stage or high-risk work, describe how feasibility will be established and the risk managed. Name any hazardous procedures, situations or materials and the precautions taken. A timeline by aim is customary and helps reviewers judge feasibility. Do not put the Data Management and Sharing Plan, inclusion enrollment, vertebrate animal or authentication-of-key-resources details here; each has its own attachment, so refer to it in a phrase if needed.
elements: Sub-section for each aim matching the Specific Aims page
Design, methods and analysis plan for each aim
Rigor: controls, randomisation/blinding, sample size and power, biological variables such as sex
Preliminary studies demonstrating feasibility (expected for most R01s)
Expected results, potential problems and alternative strategies for each aim
Benchmarks for success for each aim
Hazardous procedures and precautions identified, if any
Timeline by aim
sourcesNeeded: Statistical analysis or power analysis notes
Letters or descriptions of key resources, cores or collaborators
dataNeeded: Preliminary results with sample sizes and effect sizes
Power calculation inputs (effect size, alpha, power, attrition)
Project timeline by aim and year

sections.heading: Progress Report
sections.guidance: Include only for a renewal application. Give the beginning and ending dates of the period covered since the last competitive review, summarise the specific aims of that period and the importance of the findings, and give a succinct account of published and unpublished results toward each aim, including negative results and any change to the aims with the reason for it. Keep it factual and link the results to the new aims they motivate. NIH allows it as its own sub-heading of the Research Strategy; it counts toward the page limit. The publication list goes in the separate Progress Report Publication List attachment, not here.
sections.lengthHint: Counts toward the Research Strategy page limit
elements: Dates of the project period covered
Original aims summarised
Progress, key results and their importance reported for each prior aim
Changes to aims, and negative results, explained
Link from prior results to the new aims
sourcesNeeded: Publications and products from the prior period
dataNeeded: Project period start and end dates
Key quantitative results from the prior period

rubric.criterion: NIH Factor 1, Importance of the Research (Significance and Innovation), on the NIH 1-9 scale where 1 is best: does the work address an important gap, rest on rigorous prior research, and bring something genuinely new?

levels.descriptor: Exceptional: an important, clearly defined gap; prior research is critically and fairly assessed; innovation is concrete and substantial; essentially no weaknesses.
Outstanding: extremely strong importance and innovation with only negligible weaknesses.
Excellent: very strong case for importance and novelty with only some minor weaknesses.
Very good: strong overall, but numerous minor weaknesses, such as a gap stated more broadly than the aims address.
Good: strong in places but with at least one moderate weakness, such as a thin assessment of the rigor of prior work or an incremental innovation.
Satisfactory: some strengths but some moderate weaknesses; the reviewer has to infer why the work matters.
Fair: some strengths but at least one major weakness, such as no clear gap or innovation claims that are really established methods.
Marginal: a few strengths and a few major weaknesses; importance and novelty are mostly asserted rather than shown.
Poor: very few strengths and numerous major weaknesses; the problem, gap or novelty is missing or unconvincing.

rubric.criterion: NIH Factor 2, Rigor and Feasibility (Approach), on the NIH 1-9 scale where 1 is best: are the design, methods and analysis rigorous, and can the aims realistically be achieved?

levels.descriptor: Exceptional: every aim has a rigorous design with appropriate controls, justified sample size and attention to biological variables; preliminary data show feasibility; pitfalls, alternatives, benchmarks and timeline are clear; essentially no weaknesses.
Outstanding: extremely strong rigor and feasibility with only negligible weaknesses.
Excellent: very strong rigor and feasibility with only some minor weaknesses.
Very good: strong, but with numerous minor weaknesses, such as an alternative strategy that is named but not developed.
Good: strong in places but with at least one moderate weakness, such as an unjustified sample size or an aim that depends on another succeeding.
Satisfactory: workable plan with some moderate weaknesses in controls, analysis or timeline.
Fair: at least one major weakness, such as no power analysis, missing controls or no preliminary evidence of feasibility.
Marginal: a few strengths and a few major weaknesses; the reviewer doubts the aims can be completed as described.
Poor: very few strengths and numerous major weaknesses; methods are vague, unrigorous or unlikely to answer the question.

rubric.criterion: NIH Factor 3, Expertise and Resources, which NIH rates only sufficient or insufficient (scored here 1 = sufficient, 2 = insufficient so that, as for Factors 1 and 2, the lower score is better): as far as these sections show, do the team's expertise, preliminary work and stated resources fit the proposed methods?

levels.descriptor: Sufficient: the methods are ones the team has shown it can carry out (preliminary data, prior publications, named cores or collaborators), and no proposed work lacks an evident source of expertise or resources.
Insufficient: key methods have no evident expertise, preliminary work or resource behind them, or the text relies on capabilities the application does not establish.

rubric.criterion: Aims alignment: the Specific Aims page and the Research Strategy tell one consistent story, with the same aims, hypotheses and outcomes throughout.

levels.descriptor: Every aim on the Specific Aims page has a matching Approach sub-section with the same number, title and hypothesis; Significance and Innovation support those exact aims; expected outcomes agree everywhere.
Aims and strategy match, with small drift such as a renamed aim or an outcome mentioned in one place only.
Noticeable mismatches: an aim lacks a matching Approach sub-section, hypotheses are worded differently, or Significance argues for a different problem than the aims address.
The aims and the strategy describe different projects, or the aims cannot be traced through the Research Strategy at all.

title: NSF Project Description, Broader Impacts and Data Management and Sharing Plan
summary: The core of a U.S. National Science Foundation proposal: a Project Description of 15 pages or fewer with objectives, relation to current knowledge, the plan of work, a separate Broader Impacts section and, when required, Results from Prior NSF Support, plus the Data Management and Sharing Plan (DMSP) built in Research.gov. Reviewers judge it on Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts.
audience: An NSF merit review panel and ad hoc reviewers, usually scientists in or near the field, plus the program officer who makes the recommendation; they read many proposals and look for the two merit review criteria and the five review elements.
tone: Clear, concrete and confident scientific prose, readable by a scientist outside the subfield; specific about what will be done and how success will be measured, never promotional.
preamble: You are an experienced NSF-funded principal investigator drafting the Project Description and Data Management and Sharing Plan of an NSF proposal under PAPPG 24-1 as amended by Supplement 2 (NSF 26-202). Reviewers judge two criteria, Intellectual Merit (the potential to advance knowledge) and Broader Impacts (the potential to benefit society), on five elements: the potential of the activity, its creativity and originality, a well-reasoned plan with a mechanism to assess success, the qualifications of the team, and the adequacy of resources. Write so each element can be found. The program solicitation governs where it differs from the PAPPG: if one is linked, follow its page limits, required sections and extra review criteria. The whole Project Description, including figures and Results from Prior NSF Support, must fit in 15 pages unless the solicitation says otherwise; it must be self-contained and contain no URLs; and Broader Impacts must be a separate section with "Broader Impacts" as a heading on its own line. Broader Impacts activities must be specific (who does what, with what resources, and how success is measured) and open to all Americans; do not limit participation by a protected characteristic. Keep the data types, methods and sharing in the DMSP consistent with the research plan. Do not invent preliminary results, publications, prior award numbers or amounts, collaborators, partner institutions, facilities, participant counts or data repositories; where a fact is missing from the sources, write a marked placeholder such as [prior award number needed]. Do not move narrative into References or other documents to get around the page limit.

sections.heading: Overview and Objectives
sections.guidance: Open with the problem and why it matters now, then state the project's goal and two to four specific objectives or research questions for the award period. Say in a sentence each what will be learned or built and what difference it makes, so a reviewer can find the Intellectual Merit claim in the first half page. Name the expected significance plainly: the advance in knowledge if the objectives are met. Preview the Broader Impacts in one sentence and point to the section. Common failures: a long literature preamble before the objectives appear, objectives that are activities ("we will collect data") rather than outcomes, and claims of transformation with no stated mechanism.
elements: Problem and why it matters stated in the opening paragraph
Overall goal of the project
2-4 specific objectives or research questions for the award period
Expected significance: the advance in knowledge if the objectives are met
One-sentence preview of the Broader Impacts
dataNeeded: Award period and requested start date

sections.heading: Background and Relation to Current Knowledge
sections.guidance: Place the project against the current state of knowledge: what is known, what is contested and the specific gap this project addresses. Relate it to the PI's own work in progress under other support and say what is new here, so reviewers see the project is neither duplicating nor merely extending existing awards. Include preliminary results only where they show the approach can work, with figures sized to earn their space. Common failures: a survey of the field that never names the gap; preliminary data presented without saying what it proves; no mention of related current support that reviewers will see in the Current and Pending forms.
elements: Current state of knowledge summarized with citations
Specific gap or open question the project addresses
Relation to the PI's work in progress under other support
Preliminary results showing feasibility, where available
What is creative, original or potentially transformative about the approach
sourcesNeeded: Peer-reviewed literature on the state of the field

sections.heading: Research Plan
sections.guidance: Organize by objective, using the same numbering as the overview. For each, give the rationale, the design of the activities, and the methods and procedures where appropriate, with enough detail that a reviewer can judge the plan well reasoned and well organized. Name the data, samples, software or other products each activity produces, because the DMSP must account for them. State the risks to each objective and the alternative you would use, and how the objectives depend on one another. Common failures: methods described at a level a reviewer cannot evaluate; a plan that does not map to the objectives; data types appearing here that the DMSP never mentions.
elements: Sub-section for each objective matching the overview
Design, methods and procedures for each objective
Data and research products each activity produces
Risks and alternative approaches
Dependencies between objectives addressed
sourcesNeeded: Letters of collaboration describing partner roles
dataNeeded: Sample sizes or scale of data collection

sections.heading: Evaluation Plan and Timeline
sections.guidance: Say how you will know whether the project succeeded: for each objective, the measurable outcome or benchmark and how it will be assessed, which answers review element 3's mechanism to assess success. Include a timeline by year or quarter for the research and the Broader Impacts activities, with milestones a program officer can check in annual reports. Where a solicitation asks for an external evaluator or a management plan, say who and how. Common failures: a timeline with no milestones; success defined as "publishing papers"; Broader Impacts left out of the timeline.
sections.lengthHint: About half a page to 1 page
elements: Measurable outcome or benchmark for each objective
How and when success will be assessed
Timeline by year or quarter with milestones
Broader Impacts activities included in the timeline
sourcesNeeded: Solicitation evaluation or management requirements, if any

sections.heading: Broader Impacts
sections.guidance: This heading must appear on its own line, exactly as "Broader Impacts". Describe how the project benefits society: through the research itself, activities tied directly to it, or complementary activities the project supports. For each activity name what will be done, who carries it out, who it reaches, the resources behind it (partners, budget, staff time) and how success will be measured. Activities for participation, outreach or recruitment must be open to all Americans; do not limit eligibility by a protected characteristic (NSF priorities statement, April 18, 2025). Scale ambitions to the budget and team. Common failures: intentions with no plan to assess them ("we will engage the public"); activities with no named lead or partner; a list of generic outreach unrelated to the research.
elements: "Broader Impacts" heading on its own line
Specific named activities and the societal outcome each serves
Who carries out each activity, and partners
Resources committed to each activity
How success of each activity is assessed
Activities open to all, with no eligibility limited by protected characteristic
sourcesNeeded: Institutional programs or facilities used for the activities
dataNeeded: Expected reach (participants, users, schools) with its basis
Budget or staff time for the activities

sections.heading: Project Team and Management
sections.guidance: Include when there are several senior personnel, institutions or a collaborative proposal, or when the solicitation asks for a management or collaboration plan. Say who leads each objective and activity, why they are qualified (with a phrase each, not a biosketch), how the team coordinates and decides, and the resources at the home organization or through collaborations that make the work possible. This is where review elements 4 and 5, qualifications and resources, become visible. Keep facility details in the Facilities, Equipment and Other Resources document and refer to it.
elements: Lead for each objective and activity
Qualifications tied to the methods
Coordination and decision-making across people or institutions
Resources available through the organization or collaborations

sections.heading: Results from Prior NSF Support
sections.guidance: Required when any PI or co-PI has an NSF award that ended in the past five years or any current NSF funding, including no-cost extensions; each reports only the award most closely related to this proposal. For each, give the award number, amount, period of support and title; a summary of results under two separate headings, Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts; the publications from the award with full citations (here or in References Cited) or a statement that there were none; evidence of research products and their availability, as the earlier data plan described; and, for a renewal, how the completed work relates to the proposed work. A recent award with no results yet describes its major goals and broader impacts. Keep it to five pages or fewer; it counts toward the 15. Never invent an award number, amount or result.
sections.lengthHint: 5 pages or fewer; counts toward the 15
elements: Award number, amount and period of support
Project title
Intellectual Merit results under its own heading
Broader Impacts results under its own heading
Publications from the award, or a statement that there were none
Research products and their availability
Relation to the proposed work (renewals)

sections.heading: Data Management and Sharing Plan
sections.guidance: Draft the DMSP here, then enter it in the Research.gov DMSP tool (required for proposals since April 27, 2026; it is not part of the 15-page Project Description). Check the tool and the solicitation for any length limit; NSF 26-202 and NSF Engineering's guidance still refer to a two-page limit. Data management material that does not fit may use part of the 15-page Project Description, but do not use the DMSP to get around the Project Description page limit. NSF Engineering's guidance lists the tool's prompts for each data or research product category: the category itself; access policies and limitations; data standards and metadata; provenance; public archiving; timeline for public accessibility; data availability; and accountability (the senior personnel responsible). Use one block per category and confirm the prompts in the live form, since directorates may differ. Data supporting publications must be shared at publication; justify any exception here at submission. A collaborative proposal or one with subawards carries one combined plan. Saying no detailed plan is needed requires a clear justification. Reviewers assess the DMSP under Intellectual Merit, Broader Impacts or both, so every data type named in the Research Plan should appear here. Do not name a repository, standard or embargo the sources do not support; mark it [repository to confirm].
sections.lengthHint: Entered in Research.gov; check the solicitation for limits
elements: One entry per data or research product category
Access policies and limitations for each category
Data standards and metadata
Provenance of each category
Public archiving: where products are deposited
Timeline for public accessibility, with publication data shared at publication
Data availability and retention
Accountability: senior personnel responsible
Exceptions to sharing described and justified
dataNeeded: Data types and estimated volumes from the Research Plan

rubric.criterion: Intellectual Merit: the potential to advance knowledge, judged on potential, creativity and originality, a well-reasoned plan with a mechanism to assess success, qualifications and resources.

levels.descriptor: Objectives address a clearly stated gap; the approach is original; the plan maps to each objective with measurable benchmarks; the team and resources visibly fit the methods.
Strong case with minor gaps, such as one objective without a benchmark or originality asserted more than shown.
The gap or the plan is vague in places; success is not measurable for some objectives; qualifications or resources for key methods are unclear.
No clear gap or plan; objectives are activities; nothing shows how success will be judged.

rubric.criterion: Broader Impacts: specific activities with a named lead, resources, reach and assessment, open to all, under a 'Broader Impacts' heading of its own.

levels.descriptor: Each activity names what, who, the resources and how success is measured; the outcomes are plausible for the budget; the heading stands alone; participation is open to all.
Activities are specific but one lacks a lead, resources or an assessment.
Mostly intentions; little on who carries them out or how they are assessed.
Generic or missing; no separate heading; or eligibility limited by a protected characteristic.

rubric.criterion: DMSP consistency: the plan covers every data and product type the Research Plan names, follows the tool's prompts, and shares publication data at publication or justifies the exception.

levels.descriptor: Every data type in the Research Plan has an entry with access, standards, archiving, timeline and accountability; exceptions are justified.
Complete for the main data types; a minor product or prompt is thin.
Some data types named in the methods are missing, or the timeline or responsibility is unclear.
Generic boilerplate that contradicts or ignores the methods.

rubric.criterion: Results from Prior NSF Support: complete PAPPG items, Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts under separate headings, within five pages.

levels.descriptor: Award number, amount, period, title, separate Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts results, publications and products all present; within five pages.
One required item is missing or the two headings are merged.
Several items missing, results unrelated to the award, or over five pages.
