title: Policy decision memo
summary: A short internal memo that asks a senior decision-maker to make one specific decision, or to approve a recommendation. It puts the decision and the recommendation first, then gives the background, the problem, two to four options with their trade-offs, and the next steps. It is written in plain language so a busy reader can act on the first paragraph alone.
audience: A senior official or executive (director, minister, board chair, agency head) who has little time, knows the organisation but not the details of this issue, and must make or approve a decision.
tone: Plain, direct and neutral: short sentences, active voice, "we" for the writing office and "you" for the decision-maker; even-handed on options, then clear and confident in the recommendation.
preamble: You are an experienced policy adviser writing a decision memo for a senior decision-maker. Follow plain-language practice: lead with what the reader must decide, use short sentences and paragraphs, active voice, everyday words, and "you" for the reader and "we" for the writing office. Define each acronym on first use, or avoid it. One memo asks for one decision; if the material contains several, say so in the Bottom Line Up Front and keep the memo to the main one. Present every option fairly, including doing nothing when that is a real option, and describe each with the same headings (what it is, pros, cons, cost, risk) so options can be compared side by side. Keep analysis (Background, Issue, Options) separate from advocacy (Recommendation): apart from naming it in the Bottom Line Up Front, do not argue for the recommended option before the Recommendation section. Make the recommendation name exactly one option (or, if the analysis supports it, a stated combination of named options) and use the same wording as the decision requested in the Bottom Line Up Front. Give amounts, dates and deadlines as specific figures; where a figure is not in the material, write a placeholder such as "[cost estimate needed]" rather than estimating. Do not invent stakeholders' positions, legal authorities or precedents. The whole memo should normally fit on two pages, excluding attachments.

sections.heading: Memo header
sections.guidance: The routing block that identifies the memo. Fill in who the memo is for (name and title), who it is from (name, title and office), the date, and a subject line. The subject line should name the decision, not just the topic, for example "Decision needed: extend the pilot grant programme to rural counties". Add a decision deadline when the decision is time-bound.
elements: Recipient name and title
Sender name, title and office
Date
Subject line that names the decision
sections.scaffold:
**To:** [Name, title]
**From:** [Name, title, office]
**Date:** [Date]
**Subject:** Decision needed: [the decision in a few words]
**Decision needed by:** [Date, if time-bound]

sections.heading: Bottom Line Up Front
sections.guidance: State in the first sentence exactly what the reader is being asked to decide or approve, and by when. In the next sentence or two give the recommendation and the single most important reason for it, including the headline cost or impact. A reader who stops here should be able to act. Do not open with background or history.
elements: The specific decision or approval requested
Deadline or reason the decision is needed now
The recommended option, named
The main reason for the recommendation
Headline cost or impact

sections.heading: Background
sections.guidance: Give only the context the decision-maker needs to understand the options: how the issue arose, what policy or programme is in place now, relevant legal or budget authority, and any earlier decisions on the matter. Cite the sources for facts and figures. Leave out history that does not bear on the choice. A short bulleted list of key facts is often clearer than paragraphs.
elements: How the issue arose
Current policy, programme or practice
Relevant legal, regulatory or budget authority
Prior decisions or commitments on the matter

sections.heading: Issue
sections.guidance: Define the problem the decision must solve, in concrete terms: who is affected, how much, and what happens if nothing is done. Quantify the scale with evidence where you can. Note the constraints any option must respect (budget, law, timing), since the Recommendation will be judged against them, and the positions of key stakeholders where the material documents them; if none are documented, say so rather than guessing. Stay neutral; do not argue for an option here.
elements: Problem statement in one or two sentences
Who is affected and the scale, with evidence
Consequence of taking no action
Constraints any option must meet (budget, legal, timing)
Stakeholder positions, or a note that none are documented
sourcesNeeded: Data or evidence on the problem's scale
dataNeeded: Number of people or organisations affected

sections.heading: Options
sections.guidance: Set out two to four real, distinct options (each a choice the reader could make on its own), including the status quo when doing nothing is a genuine choice. Give each a short descriptive name and the same parts in the same order: what it involves, pros, cons, cost, and risk (including implementation and legal risk). Be even-handed: give the strongest case for each option, and do not signal the recommendation yet. When options are many or the comparison is close, add a small comparison table after the descriptions.
elements: Two to four distinct options, each named
Status quo or no-action option included, or a reason it is not viable
Pros and cons for every option
Cost estimate for every option
Risks for every option
Same structure used for each option
sourcesNeeded: Evaluations or examples of similar policies elsewhere

sections.heading: Recommendation
sections.guidance: Name the recommended option and explain why it is better than the others against the constraints set out in the Issue section. Acknowledge its main drawback and how it would be managed. The recommendation must match the decision requested in the Bottom Line Up Front. End with a clear decision line the reader can mark, such as "Approve / Disapprove / Discuss".
elements: One recommended option, named
Reasons it outperforms the alternatives
Main drawback and how it will be managed
Consistent with the Bottom Line Up Front
Decision line (Approve / Disapprove / Discuss)

sections.heading: Implementation and Next Steps
sections.guidance: Say what happens once the decision is made: the concrete actions, who owns each, and when it is due. Mention any approvals, consultations, notices or announcements needed, and how progress or success will be measured. A short numbered list or a small table of action, owner and date works best.
elements: Concrete actions after approval
Owner for each action
Dates or milestones
Further approvals, consultation or communications needed
How success will be measured

sections.heading: Attachments and References
sections.guidance: List the supporting documents attached to the memo and the key sources cited, so the reader can check the detail without it cluttering the memo. Give each attachment a letter and a descriptive title, and note who was consulted or cleared the memo if your organisation requires it.
elements: Lettered list of attachments with descriptive titles
Key sources cited
Offices consulted or clearances, where required
sourcesNeeded: Supporting analyses, data tables or drafts referred to in the memo

rubric.criterion: Decision up front: the reader learns from the opening what they must decide, by when, and what is recommended.

levels.descriptor: The first sentence states the specific decision requested and its deadline; the recommendation, its main reason and the headline cost follow immediately. The reader could act on this section alone.
The decision and recommendation are in the opening section but are vague, slightly out of order, or missing the deadline or headline cost.
The opening starts with background, or the decision is implied rather than stated; the reader must read further to learn what is being asked.
No clear decision request anywhere near the top, or the memo informs without asking for a decision at all.

rubric.criterion: Problem defined: the Issue section states the problem, its scale and the constraints, neutrally and with evidence.

levels.descriptor: States the problem in one or two sentences, quantifies who is affected with cited evidence, says what happens if nothing is done, and lists the budget, legal and timing constraints the options must meet, without arguing for any option.
Problem and consequences are clear, but the scale is unquantified or uncited, or the constraints are incomplete.
The problem is described only in general terms or mixed with background, constraints are absent, or the section already argues for a solution.
No identifiable problem statement; the memo moves from background straight to options.

rubric.criterion: Options fairly presented: real, distinct alternatives compared on the same terms.

levels.descriptor: Two to four genuine, distinct options, including no action where relevant, each described with the same parts (what, pros, cons, cost, risk). Each is given its strongest case and the recommendation is not signalled early.
Real options with mostly consistent treatment; one option has thinner analysis, or a cost or risk is missing for one option.
Options are lopsided: straw-man alternatives, overlapping options, or the analysis argues for one option throughout. Costs or risks are missing for several options.
Only one option is offered, or options are listed without trade-offs, so the reader has no real choice.

rubric.criterion: Recommendation justified and consistent: one clear choice, reasoned against the alternatives and matching the request.

levels.descriptor: Names exactly one option (or a stated combination), explains why it beats the alternatives against the stated constraints, owns its main drawback, matches the Bottom Line Up Front, and ends with a decision line.
A clear recommendation with sound reasons, but the comparison with alternatives is thin or the drawback is not addressed.
The recommendation is hedged or differs in wording or substance from the opening request; reasons restate the option's merits without comparison.
No recommendation, several competing recommendations, or one that contradicts the analysis or the opening.

rubric.criterion: Actionability: the reader knows exactly what happens after the decision, who does it and when.

levels.descriptor: Every next step has an owner and a date; required approvals, consultation and communications are named, and success measures are stated.
Next steps are concrete actions, but some lack an owner or a date, or required approvals or success measures are missing.
Next steps are general intentions ("work with partners", "monitor progress") without owners or timing.
No next steps, or the memo ends without saying how the decision would be carried out.

provenance.source: Federal Plain Language Guidelines (digital.gov, formerly plainlanguage.gov) for the writing rules; section structure, guidance and rubric hand-written from common government decision-memo practice
provenance.license: Public domain (US government); section list, guidance and rubric are own text

title: Product Requirements Document (PRD)
summary: A product requirements document defines a problem worth solving, who has it, and what a product or feature must do to solve it, before design and engineering commit to a solution. It sets goals and non-goals, prioritised functional and non-functional requirements, success metrics and a release scope, so product, design, engineering and stakeholders can agree on what will be built and how success will be judged.
signals: As a <user>, I want <capability> so that <benefit>
must have / should have / could have
audience: Product managers, designers, engineers, QA and business stakeholders who must agree on what is being built, for whom, and how success will be measured.
tone: Direct, specific and testable: plain declarative statements, decisions stated as decisions, and no marketing language.
preamble: You are an experienced product manager writing a product requirements document that a cross-functional team will build from and sign off on. Describe the problem and the required behaviour, not the implementation: say what the product must do and why, and leave how to the design and engineering documents unless a constraint is genuinely fixed. Write every requirement so someone could test it: one behaviour per requirement, a stable identifier (FR-1, NFR-1), a priority, and observable acceptance criteria; replace vague words such as fast, easy, intuitive or robust with measurable thresholds. Tie each goal to a metric with a baseline and a target, and each requirement back to a user story or goal. State non-goals and exclusions explicitly. Do not invent user research findings, metrics, baselines, dates, owners or commitments; where the sources do not supply them, write a clearly marked placeholder (for example [TBD: baseline conversion rate]) and list the gap under Open Questions. Use tables for requirement lists, metrics and risks when they have more than three rows.

sections.heading: Overview and Problem Statement
sections.guidance: Open with two or three sentences a busy stakeholder could read alone: what is being proposed, for whom, and why now. Then state the problem from the user's point of view, with the evidence that it is real and how often or how badly it occurs (support tickets, research findings, usage data, revenue at risk). Describe how users cope today and why that is not good enough. Keep proposed solutions out of the problem statement; a reader should be able to agree with the problem before they see the answer.
elements: One-paragraph summary of what is proposed, for whom and why now
Problem stated from the user's perspective, without naming a solution
Evidence of the problem's size or frequency (data, research or feedback)
Current workaround or status quo and why it falls short
Link to the business or strategic objective the work supports
dataNeeded: Number of affected users or accounts
Frequency or cost of the problem
Relevant funnel, usage or revenue figures

sections.heading: Goals and Non-Goals
sections.guidance: List three to five goals as outcomes for users or the business, not as features to ship. Each goal should be specific enough that the Success Metrics section can measure it. Then list non-goals: things a reasonable reader might expect this work to cover that it deliberately will not, each with a one-line reason. Non-goals prevent scope creep and settle debates early, so name the tempting adjacent problems explicitly.
elements: 3-5 goals phrased as user or business outcomes, not features
Each goal traceable to a success metric
Explicit non-goals with a short reason for each
Goals ranked or prioritised when they could conflict

sections.heading: Users and Personas
sections.guidance: Identify the primary user the product is designed for and any secondary users or affected roles (administrators, buyers, support staff). For each persona give their context, the job they are trying to get done, their current pain, and any constraint that shapes the requirements (skill level, device, accessibility needs, permissions, regulation). Base personas on research where the sources provide it and say so; mark assumed personas as assumptions. Note who is explicitly not a target user.
sections.lengthHint: 1-3 personas, a short paragraph or table row each
elements: Primary persona with context, goal and current pain
Secondary users or affected roles identified
Constraints that shape requirements (device, skill, accessibility, permissions)
Evidence basis for each persona, or marked as an assumption
Users explicitly out of scope

sections.heading: User Stories and Use Cases
sections.guidance: Write the key user stories in the form "As a <persona>, I want <capability> so that <benefit>", grouped by persona or workflow and numbered so requirements can refer to them. For the main workflows, add a short use-case narrative covering the trigger, the steps the user takes, and the end state. Include at least one edge or failure case (no data, lost connection, permission denied, wrong input) for each core flow. Keep stories about user intent; detailed system behaviour belongs in Functional Requirements.
elements: Stories in "As a / I want / so that" form, each numbered
Stories cover every primary persona
Main workflow described end to end (trigger, steps, end state)
Edge and failure cases for core flows
Each story mapped to a goal

sections.heading: Functional Requirements
sections.guidance: List what the product must do, one behaviour per requirement, each with a stable ID (FR-1, FR-2), a priority (Must / Should / Could, or P0 / P1 / P2) and the user story it serves. Give each requirement acceptance criteria a tester could check, ideally in Given / When / Then form. Use a table (ID, requirement, priority, story, acceptance criteria) when there are more than three. State requirements as observable behaviour ("The system shows an error and keeps the user's input when payment fails"), not implementation ("Use a retry queue"). Make sure the Must set alone delivers a coherent first release.
elements: Every requirement has a unique ID
Every requirement has a priority (Must/Should/Could or P0-P2)
Testable acceptance criteria for each requirement
Each requirement traced to a user story or goal
Error, empty and permission states specified
Must-have set defines a coherent minimum release

sections.heading: Non-Functional Requirements
sections.guidance: Specify the qualities the product must have, each with a measurable threshold and an ID (NFR-1, NFR-2): performance (for example 95th-percentile response time), availability, scalability, security and privacy, accessibility (name the standard, such as WCAG 2.2 AA), localisation, compatibility (browsers, devices, operating systems) and compliance. Include only categories that matter for this product, but say so when a usually relevant one is deliberately not applicable. Replace adjectives with numbers and conditions.
elements: Performance targets with measurable thresholds
Security and privacy requirements, including data handling
Accessibility standard named (e.g. WCAG 2.2 AA)
Supported platforms, browsers or devices
Reliability or availability target
Applicable legal or compliance requirements

sections.heading: Success Metrics
sections.guidance: Define how the team will know the product worked. Name one primary metric and a small number of secondary metrics, each with a current baseline, a target, a time frame and the data source. Add guardrail metrics that must not get worse (for example support contact rate, latency, churn). Tie each metric to a goal and say how it will be measured (instrumentation, experiment design, survey). If a baseline is unknown, say how and when it will be established rather than inventing one.
elements: One primary metric tied to the main goal
Baseline and target for every metric
Time frame for reaching each target
Guardrail metrics that must not regress
Measurement method and data source for each metric
dataNeeded: Current baseline values for each metric

sections.heading: Scope and Release Plan
sections.guidance: State what is in the first release (MVP) and what is deferred to later phases, referring to requirement IDs rather than restating them. Lay out the phases or milestones with target dates where they are known and the criteria for moving between them. Describe the rollout approach (internal dogfood, beta, staged percentage, feature flag, general availability) and the launch criteria that must be met before release. Mark dates as targets unless they are committed.
elements: MVP scope listed by requirement ID
Deferred items and the phase they move to
Milestones or phases with target dates
Rollout approach (beta, staged rollout, feature flag, GA)
Launch criteria that must be met before release

sections.heading: Dependencies and Risks
sections.guidance: List the teams, systems, vendors, approvals and decisions this work depends on, with an owner and the date each is needed by. Then list the main risks (technical, market, legal, operational, adoption), each with its likelihood, impact and a mitigation or contingency. Include assumptions that, if wrong, would change the plan. A table with columns for risk, likelihood, impact, mitigation and owner works well.
elements: Internal and external dependencies with owners
Date each dependency is needed by
Risks rated for likelihood and impact
Mitigation or contingency for each significant risk
Key assumptions stated explicitly

sections.heading: Open Questions
sections.guidance: List the unresolved questions that block or could change the requirements, each with an owner and a date by which it needs an answer. Include every placeholder or gap left elsewhere in the document. When a question is answered, write the decision into the section it affects and keep a one-line record here (question, decision, date) so reviewers can see what changed.
elements: Each open question stated specifically
Owner assigned to each question
Date by which an answer is needed
Placeholders and gaps from other sections carried here
Answered questions kept as a one-line record of the decision and date

rubric.criterion: Problem definition: the problem, the affected users and the evidence for it are clear and kept separate from the solution.

levels.descriptor: The problem is stated from the user's point of view, its size or frequency is backed by data or research, the primary and secondary users are clearly identified, and the solution is kept out of the problem statement. A stakeholder could agree the problem matters before reading further.
The problem and users are clear, but the supporting evidence is thin or partly anecdotal, or the problem statement leans slightly towards a particular solution.
The problem is described vaguely or mainly as a missing feature; users are generic ("all users"); evidence is absent or asserted without support.
There is no identifiable user problem; the document starts from a solution, or the problem and users cannot be determined.

rubric.criterion: Requirement testability: each requirement describes one observable behaviour or quality with acceptance criteria or a measurable threshold.

levels.descriptor: Every requirement has an ID, describes a single observable behaviour or a measurable quality, and has acceptance criteria a tester could verify without asking the author. Error, empty and permission states are covered, and no vague qualities (fast, easy, intuitive) remain.
Most requirements are testable, but a few lack acceptance criteria, bundle several behaviours, or use a vague quality without a threshold.
Many requirements are vague, compound or written as implementation instructions; acceptance criteria are missing for much of the list; edge cases are largely absent.
Requirements are a loose feature wish list that could not be built or tested without substantial further clarification.

rubric.criterion: Prioritisation and scope control: priorities, non-goals and release scope make clear what will and will not be built first.

levels.descriptor: Every requirement carries a priority, the must-have set forms a coherent first release, non-goals are explicit with reasons, and the release plan names what is deferred and the criteria for each phase.
Priorities and scope are mostly clear, but some requirements lack a priority, non-goals are thin, or the boundary between the first release and later phases is fuzzy.
Most items are marked top priority or not prioritised at all; non-goals are missing; the first release cannot be distinguished from the full vision.
There is no prioritisation or scope boundary; the document implies everything ships at once.

rubric.criterion: Measurable outcomes and traceability: goals are tied to metrics with baselines and targets, and requirements trace back to goals and user stories.

levels.descriptor: Each goal maps to a metric with a baseline, target, time frame and data source; guardrail metrics are defined; every requirement traces to a user story or goal, and no requirement lacks a reason to exist.
Goals have metrics, but some lack baselines, targets or a measurement method, or traceability from requirements to goals is incomplete.
Metrics are vanity or activity measures, or are listed without baselines or targets; most requirements cannot be traced to a goal.
There is no way to judge whether the product succeeded; goals and metrics are missing or unrelated to the requirements.

title: Proposal
summary: A proposal asks a decision-maker or funder to approve a piece of work: it summarizes the request, explains why it is needed, sets objectives, and describes the approach, timeline, budget and how success will be judged. Use it for internal project proposals, partnership pitches and small funding requests that do not follow a funder's own template.
audience: A decision-maker, sponsor or funder who must decide whether to approve and resource the proposed work, and who knows the organisation but not the details.
tone: Confident, concrete and persuasive without hype; specific about what will be done, by when and at what cost.
preamble: You are an experienced writer drafting a proposal for a decision-maker who must approve and resource the work. Lead with what is being asked for and why it matters. Be concrete: name deliverables, dates, owners and amounts. Make every objective specific and measurable, and make the approach, timeline, budget and evaluation consistent with the objectives and with each other. Where an amount, date or name is not in the material, write a placeholder such as "[budget figure needed]" rather than estimating. Do not overstate benefits or promise outcomes the material does not support.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.guidance: In one short paragraph, state what is proposed, the problem or opportunity it addresses, the expected result, and what is being asked of the reader (approval, funding, people) with the headline cost and duration. A reader who stops here should know what they are being asked to decide.
elements: What is proposed
Problem or opportunity addressed
Expected result
The ask: approval, funding or resources
Headline cost and duration

sections.heading: Reason for Proposal
sections.guidance: Explain why the work is needed now. Describe the current situation and its cost or risk, the evidence for the need, who is affected, and what happens if nothing is done. Ground the case in the sources and give figures where they exist.
elements: Current situation
Evidence of the need
Who is affected
Consequence of doing nothing
sourcesNeeded: Evidence of the problem or opportunity

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.guidance: List two to five objectives the work will achieve. Make each specific and measurable, with a target and a date, and tie each to the need described above. Use a numbered list.
elements: Two to five numbered objectives
Measurable target for each objective
Target date for each objective
Link from each objective to the need

sections.heading: Approach
sections.guidance: Describe how the objectives will be met: the main activities, who will carry them out, the methods or tools, and the deliverables each activity produces. Explain why this approach was chosen over the obvious alternatives, and name the key risks and how they will be managed.
elements: Main activities
Who will do the work
Deliverables
Why this approach over alternatives
Key risks and mitigations

sections.heading: Timeline
sections.guidance: Lay out the schedule from start to finish as phases or milestones with dates, and mark dependencies and decision points. A Markdown table (milestone, date, deliverable) works well.
elements: Start and end dates
Milestones with dates
Dependencies and decision points

sections.heading: Budget
sections.guidance: Give the total cost and its breakdown by major category (people, equipment, services, other), with the basis for each figure. Note any cost already committed, any contribution from other sources, and ongoing costs after the work ends. Present the breakdown as a Markdown table.
elements: Total cost
Breakdown by category
Basis for each figure
Ongoing costs after the work ends

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.guidance: Explain how success will be judged: the measures for each objective, how and when they will be collected, who will review them, and how results will be reported back to the reader.
elements: Success measures for each objective
How and when data will be collected
Who reviews the results
How results will be reported

rubric.criterion: Objectives, approach, timeline, budget and evaluation agree with each other.

levels.descriptor: Every objective has activities in the approach, milestones in the timeline, costs in the budget and a measure in the evaluation.
Mostly consistent; one objective lacks a milestone, cost line or measure.
Several gaps or contradictions between objectives, schedule, budget and evaluation.
The sections describe different projects or contradict each other.

rubric.criterion: The reader knows exactly what is being asked of them and why.

levels.descriptor: The summary states the decision, the cost and the duration, and the reason for the proposal makes a compelling, evidenced case.
The ask is clear but the case for it is thin in places.
The ask or its cost is vague, or the need is asserted rather than shown.
It is unclear what the reader is being asked to approve.

title: Review of Existing Evaluation Data (Reevaluation)
summary: A review of existing evaluation data (REED) for a student with a disability who is due for or has requested a reevaluation. It summarizes the existing data, sets it against the questions the team must answer about continued eligibility, present levels, continued need and changes to services, and proposes whether additional assessment is needed and in which areas, for the team, including the parent, to decide.
audience: The IEP team and other qualified professionals reviewing the data, including the parent, and the evaluation staff who will carry out any additional assessment.
tone: Neutral, concise and factual: each piece of data dated and sourced, plain language a parent can follow, and the proposal stated as a proposal.
preamble: You are helping an evaluation professional draft a review of existing evaluation data for a student's reevaluation. This is a DRAFT for the team, which includes the parent; the team decides what additional data, if any, it needs, and nothing in the draft decides continued eligibility, needs or services. Do not diagnose and do not state whether the student continues to have a disability; set out what the existing data shows and where it is missing, out of date or conflicting. Use federal (IDEA) terms; state forms and criteria come from the requirement set the team uses. Date and source every piece of data (who, what instrument or record, when), and say plainly when data is older than the current IEP or the last evaluation. Never carry present levels over from the last evaluation unchanged; never invent scores or dates; write "[date needed]" or "[data needed]" where the material is silent. Refer to the student as "[Student]" or by the first name already in the material, and add no identifying details beyond those already there.

sections.heading: Review Information
sections.guidance: Front matter the evaluator fills in: student placeholders, current eligibility from the last evaluation, the date of that evaluation and the three-year date, why the review is happening, and who took part. Marks the document as a draft. Not drafted by the model.
elements: Draft status stated
Current eligibility category(ies) and date of the last evaluation
Three-year reevaluation date
Reason for the review (three-year, parent or teacher request, change in needs)
Participants by role, including the parent, and whether a meeting was held
sections.scaffold:
**DRAFT for the team: a proposal, not a decision**

| Field | Entry |
|---|---|
| Student | [Student name] |
| Date of birth | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| Grade | [Grade] |
| Current eligibility category(ies) | [Category] |
| Date of last evaluation | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| Three-year reevaluation date | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| Current IEP dates | [YYYY-MM-DD to YYYY-MM-DD] |
| Reason for review | [Three-year / Parent request / Teacher request / Change in needs] |
| Review held | [In a meeting / Without a meeting] on [YYYY-MM-DD] |

**Participants**

| Role | Name |
|---|---|
| Parent or guardian | [Name] |
| Teacher(s) | [Name] |
| Evaluation staff | [Name, role] |
| Related service providers | [Name, role] |

sections.heading: Reason for Review
sections.guidance: State why the reevaluation is happening now: the three-year requirement, a request from the parent or a teacher (who and when), or a change in the student's needs or performance that the agency has noticed. Give the date of the last evaluation and what it covered, and note any new concern since then, especially one that might point to a need or disability not previously identified. Keep it short and factual.
elements: What triggered the review, with who and when
Date and scope of the last evaluation
New concerns since the last evaluation, including any that suggest a new area of need
sourcesNeeded: Parent or teacher request, if any

sections.heading: Existing Evaluation Data
sections.guidance: Summarize the existing data by source in a table (data, source, date, area, what it shows): prior evaluations and information from the parent; current classroom-based, local and state assessments and classroom-based observations; and observations by teachers and related service providers, plus progress on the current IEP goals, attendance, discipline and health, vision and hearing information where relevant. Keep each entry to what the data shows, with its date, and flag any that predates the current IEP. Follow the table with a few sentences on overall currency and gaps. Common failures: data from the last evaluation presented as current; entries with no date; a summary that skips areas related to the disability.
sections.lengthHint: A data table plus a short paragraph
elements: Prior evaluations and parent-provided information, dated
Current classroom-based, local and state assessment results, dated
Classroom-based observations and observations by teachers and providers, dated
Progress on current IEP goals
Data older than the current IEP flagged
sourcesNeeded: Teacher and related service provider observations
dataNeeded: Dates and results of each existing measure

sections.heading: Parent Input
sections.guidance: Record the parent's information and concerns for this review in their own terms: how the student is doing at home and school, changes they have noticed, questions they want the reevaluation to look at, and any outside evaluations or medical information they have shared. Say how and when the input was gathered. If input was sought but not received, say so and when it was sought.
sections.lengthHint: 1 short paragraph or a short list
elements: Parent's concerns and observations, attributed
Questions the parent wants addressed
Outside evaluations or information the parent provided
How and when input was gathered, or that it was sought and not received
sourcesNeeded: Parent input form or interview notes

sections.heading: Review of the Data by Question
sections.guidance: Take the four questions the review must address one at a time, under short sub-headings: (1) whether the student continues to have a disability and what the student's educational needs are; (2) the student's present levels of academic achievement and related developmental needs; (3) whether the student continues to need special education and related services; (4) whether any additions or changes to services are needed to meet the IEP goals and take part in the general curriculum. Under each, cite the existing data that bears on it and say whether that data is sufficient, out of date, conflicting or missing. Do not answer the eligibility question; state what the data covers and where it falls short. Common failures: "no additional data" when a new area of concern has come up; present levels taken from the last evaluation unchanged.
elements: Continued disability and educational needs: data cited and its sufficiency
Present levels and developmental needs: data cited and its sufficiency
Continued need for special education and related services: data cited and its sufficiency
Changes to services needed to meet goals: data cited and its sufficiency
Gaps, outdated or conflicting data named for each question

sections.heading: Proposed Additional Data
sections.guidance: Propose, for the team's decision, either that no additional data is needed, with the reasons drawn from the review above, or the additional data needed, listed by area (for example cognitive, academic, communication, social-emotional, adaptive, motor, health, vision, hearing) with the question each would answer and the kind of assessment or information that would provide it, in a short table. Include any area of newly suspected need. Keep both options open in the wording: this is a proposal, and the team, including the parent, decides.
elements: Proposal: no additional data needed, or additional data needed
Reasons, citing the review by question
Each proposed area with the question it would answer
Kind of assessment or information proposed for each area
Any newly suspected area of need included

sections.heading: Parent Notice and Consent
sections.guidance: Describe the next step the proposal would lead to, in plain language for the parent. If additional assessment is proposed, note that the parent's informed written consent is needed before it begins (reviewing existing data needs none). If no additional data is proposed and the team agrees, note that the parent will be told of that decision and the reasons, and of the right to ask for an assessment anyway. Mention the timeline the team's state rules set for completing a reevaluation, taken from the requirement set, without computing dates here.
elements: Consent needed before any new assessment
Notice of a no-additional-data decision, with reasons and the right to request an assessment
Next steps and who is responsible

rubric.criterion: Current, sourced data: every piece of existing data is dated and attributed, and outdated data is flagged.

levels.descriptor: Every entry names its source and date; data older than the current IEP is flagged; present levels rest on current data, not the last evaluation.
Nearly all entries are dated and sourced; one older item is not flagged.
Several entries lack dates or sources, or the last evaluation is treated as current.
Data is described in general terms with no dates or sources.

rubric.criterion: All four questions: the review addresses continued disability and needs, present levels, continued need for services, and changes to services, each with data or a named gap.

levels.descriptor: Each of the four questions has its own treatment, cites specific data, and names any gap, conflict or outdated data.
All four are addressed, but one rests on general statements.
One or more questions is missing or merged so it cannot be checked.
The questions are not addressed; the review is a list of data.

rubric.criterion: Grounded proposal: the additional-data proposal follows from the gaps found and covers any newly suspected need.

levels.descriptor: Each proposed area answers a named gap; a no-additional-data proposal gives reasons tied to the review; newly suspected needs are included.
The proposal follows from the review, but one area or reason is thin.
Proposed assessments do not match the gaps, or "no additional data" is proposed despite a new concern.
No proposal, or a blanket battery with no link to the review.

rubric.criterion: The team decides: the draft leaves the decision to the team, includes the parent's input, and states the parent's consent and notice rights.

levels.descriptor: Labelled a draft; worded as a proposal; parent input is recorded; consent for new assessment and notice of a no-data decision are both stated.
Proposal wording and parent input are present, but one right is missing.
Reads as decided, or parent input is absent.
States continued eligibility or the data decision as settled, with no parent role.

title: Research Report (IMRaD)
summary: An empirical research report in the Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion (IMRaD) structure used by journal articles, theses chapters, lab reports and technical study reports. It states a question or hypothesis, describes how data were collected and analysed in enough detail to replicate, reports findings without interpretation, and then interprets them against prior work and their limitations.
audience: Researchers and informed readers in the field, including peer reviewers, who expect enough detail to evaluate and replicate the study.
tone: Formal, precise and impersonal-but-direct scholarly prose; hedged where the evidence is uncertain, never promotional.
preamble: You are an experienced researcher writing an empirical report for peer review in the IMRaD structure. Keep each section to its job: the Introduction motivates the question and ends with the aim or hypothesis; Methods say what was done, in the past tense, with enough detail to replicate; Results report what was found, with no interpretation or speculation; the Discussion interprets. Never invent data, participants, statistics, citations or findings: where a number, sample detail or reference is not in the provided material, leave a clearly marked placeholder such as [n = ?] or [citation needed] instead of guessing. Report statistics completely (test, statistic, degrees of freedom, exact p value, effect size and confidence interval where applicable) and keep figures consistent across the Abstract, Results and Discussion. Distinguish correlation from causation, state the strength of evidence honestly, and use the field's terminology consistently once defined.

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.guidance: Write a single self-contained paragraph (or the structured Background/Methods/Results/Conclusions form if the venue requires it) that a reader can understand without the full report. Give one or two sentences each on the problem and aim, the design and sample, the main quantitative results, and the principal conclusion. Use the same numbers as the Results section, include no citations, no results absent from the body, or undefined abbreviations, and do not claim more than the Discussion supports. Draft it last, from the finished report.
elements: Problem and study aim or hypothesis
Design, sample and setting
Main results with key figures
Principal conclusion or implication
No citations or undefined abbreviations

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.guidance: Move from the broad problem to the specific question in a funnel: establish why the topic matters, summarise what prior research has shown, and identify the specific gap, contradiction or limitation this study addresses. Cite the key prior studies for each claim rather than surveying the whole literature. Close with an explicit statement of the aim, research question or testable hypotheses, so every later section can be checked against it.
elements: Importance of the problem established
Relevant prior research summarised with citations
Specific gap or unresolved question identified
Rationale linking the gap to this study
Explicit aim, research question or hypothesis
sourcesNeeded: Key prior studies in the area

sections.heading: Methods
sections.guidance: Describe what was done, in the past tense, in enough detail that a competent researcher could repeat the study. Cover the design, the participants or materials (with inclusion and exclusion criteria, recruitment and a sample size justification), the measures or instruments and their validity, the procedure in the order it happened, and the analysis plan: software and version, the test tied to each hypothesis, how missing data and exclusions were handled, and which analyses were pre-specified and which exploratory. Cite the pre-registration or protocol if there is one and follow the reporting guideline for the design where one exists (for example CONSORT for randomised trials, STROBE for observational studies, PRISMA for systematic reviews). Note ethics approval and consent for human or animal research. Use sub-headings (Participants, Materials, Procedure, Analysis) when the section is long.
elements: Study design stated
Participants or materials with selection criteria and sample size justification
Measures or instruments described
Procedure in replicable order
Statistical or analytic approach for each question
Handling of missing data and exclusions
Pre-registration or protocol cited and exploratory analyses flagged (where applicable)
Ethics approval and consent (where applicable)

sections.heading: Results
sections.guidance: Report the findings objectively, in the same order as the questions or hypotheses in the Introduction, without interpreting or explaining them. Start with the final sample and descriptive statistics, then give each analysis with complete statistics (test, statistic, degrees of freedom, exact p value, effect size and confidence interval), labelling any exploratory analyses as such. Report results that do not support the hypotheses as plainly as those that do. Use tables or figures for dense data and refer to them in the text, highlighting the key pattern instead of repeating every number.
elements: Final sample and attrition or exclusions reported
Descriptive statistics
Result for each research question or hypothesis
Complete test statistics with effect sizes
Tables or figures referenced in text
No interpretation or speculation
dataNeeded: Figures or charts of main outcomes

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.guidance: Open by restating the main finding in plain terms and answering the research question directly. Interpret what the results mean, compare them with the prior studies cited in the Introduction (agreeing and conflicting), and offer reasoned explanations for unexpected results without overstating them. State the study's limitations honestly and how they affect the conclusions, then give the practical or theoretical implications and specific directions for future research. Do not introduce new results here.
elements: Main finding restated and question answered
Interpretation of results
Comparison with prior literature
Limitations and their effect on conclusions
Practical or theoretical implications
Directions for future research

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.guidance: Use when the venue expects a separate conclusion. In one short paragraph, state the take-home message, what the study adds to the field, and the most important implication, consistent with the Discussion and no stronger than the evidence allows. Do not restate the Results in detail or add new material.
elements: Take-home message stated
Contribution to the field
Key implication, within the evidence

sections.heading: Declarations
sections.guidance: Include the statements journals and examiners expect after the main text, under their own sub-headings: funding sources and the funders' role, competing interests (state "none" explicitly if there are none), author contributions, a data and code availability statement saying where the data can be obtained or why they cannot be shared, and acknowledgements of help that does not merit authorship. Use only facts from the provided material; mark anything missing as a placeholder rather than writing a generic statement.
elements: Funding sources and funder role
Competing interests statement
Data and code availability statement
Author contributions (where the venue requires them)
dataNeeded: Data repository location or access restrictions

sections.heading: References
sections.guidance: List every work cited in the text, and only those, in one consistent citation style (APA unless the venue specifies another). Each entry needs full bibliographic details and a DOI or stable URL where available. Never add a reference that is not in the provided sources; mark any missing citation as [citation needed] in the text instead.
elements: Every in-text citation has an entry
No uncited entries
One consistent citation style
DOIs or stable URLs where available
sourcesNeeded: Full bibliographic records of cited works

rubric.criterion: Question alignment: the aim or hypothesis is explicit and every section answers to it.

levels.descriptor: The Introduction ends with a precise aim or testable hypothesis grounded in a clearly stated gap. Methods, Results and Discussion each address it in the same order, and the Abstract matches.
The aim is stated and mostly followed through, but the gap is loosely argued or one section drifts from the question.
The aim is vague or implied. Several results or analyses do not map to a stated question, or the Discussion answers a different one.
No identifiable aim or hypothesis; the sections do not connect into a single line of inquiry.

rubric.criterion: Methodological transparency: the methods are reported fully enough to evaluate and replicate.

levels.descriptor: Design, sample and selection criteria, sample size rationale, measures, procedure and an analysis plan tied to each question are all described; ethics approval is noted where needed. A peer could repeat the study.
Most details are present; one element (such as the sample size rationale or an instrument description) is thin but the study could largely be reproduced.
Important details are missing, such as selection criteria, the measures used or which test answers which question, so replication would require guessing.
Methods are sketched or absent; the reader cannot tell how the data were obtained or analysed.

rubric.criterion: Results reporting: findings are complete, accurate and kept separate from interpretation.

levels.descriptor: Every planned analysis is reported, including null or contrary results, with complete statistics and effect sizes. Tables and figures are referenced and consistent with the text. No interpretation appears in Results.
Results are complete and accurate, but some statistics lack effect sizes or intervals, or a little interpretation creeps in.
Selective or incomplete reporting: some analyses or unfavourable results are omitted, statistics are partial, or numbers disagree between sections.
Results are mostly narrative claims without supporting figures, or are mixed throughout with speculation.

rubric.criterion: Warranted interpretation: conclusions follow from the results, are placed in the literature and acknowledge limitations.

levels.descriptor: Claims match the strength of the evidence, causal language is used only where the design allows it, findings are compared with prior work including conflicting studies, and limitations are stated with their consequences.
Interpretation is mostly sound but occasionally overstated, or limitations are listed without saying how they affect the conclusions.
Conclusions frequently outrun the data, comparison with the literature is superficial, or limitations are token.
Conclusions are unsupported or contradict the results; no limitations or literature context are given.

title: Response to Reviewers
summary: A point-by-point response to peer review of a manuscript, or the Introduction to a resubmitted grant application. It summarizes the main changes, then answers every reviewer and editor comment with the change made and where, or a reasoned, evidence-based rebuttal.
audience: The original reviewers and the handling editor (or, for a grant resubmission, the new study section and program staff), who check that each point was taken seriously and find each change quickly.
tone: Courteous, specific and non-defensive; firm and evidence-based when disagreeing, never dismissive; thanks given once rather than in every reply.
preamble: You are the corresponding author or PI drafting a response to peer review. Answer every comment: keep the reviewers' numbering, quote or closely paraphrase each comment, then say what changed and exactly where (section, page or line numbers in the revised text) or, if you disagree, give the reasoning and evidence. Never claim a change the revised text does not contain, and never merge two comments so that one is lost. Keep answers to different reviewers consistent; if two reviewers ask for opposite things, say how you resolved it. Thank the reviewers once at the start, not in every reply, and avoid both flattery and defensiveness. Do not invent new analyses, results, citations or page numbers; where the author has not yet made or located a change, write a marked placeholder such as [page and line of the revision]. For an NIH resubmission, the response is the Introduction: one page for most activity codes (three for some training programs; the funding opportunity can differ). It must summarize substantial additions, deletions and changes and respond to the summary statement, and changes are outlined only there, not marked up in the application. Group points by theme and keep them terse to fit. Follow the journal's or funder's instructions where they are linked.

sections.heading: Header
sections.guidance: Identify what is being answered: the manuscript or application title, its ID or application number, the journal or funder, the date, and the corresponding author or PI. A grant Introduction usually needs no header beyond its title, so keep it short.
elements: Title and manuscript or application ID
Journal or funder
Date and corresponding author or PI
sections.scaffold:
**Response to reviewers**
**Manuscript / application:** [title] ([ID])
**Journal / funder:** [name]
**Date:** [date]
**Corresponding author / PI:** [name]

sections.heading: Summary of Changes
sections.guidance: Thank the reviewers and editor once, then summarize the main changes in a few bullets or sentences: the substantial additions, deletions and changes, each tied to the concern that prompted it. Readers who only read this should know the revision's shape. For an NIH resubmission this begins the one-page Introduction. Common failures: generic thanks repeated later; a summary that lists every minor edit; changes summarized that the revision does not contain.
elements: Thanks given once
Main changes listed
Each change tied to the concern that prompted it

sections.heading: Response to the Editor
sections.guidance: Include when the editor (or the summary statement's resume and summary of discussion) raised points of their own or set priorities among the reviews. Answer those first, in the same comment-response-change pattern, and say how conflicting reviewer requests were resolved.
elements: Each editor point answered with change and location
How conflicting reviewer requests were resolved

sections.heading: Reviewer 1
sections.guidance: Answer each of this reviewer's comments in order, keeping their numbering. For each: the comment (quoted or closely paraphrased, marked as theirs), then the response: what was changed and where (section, page or line in the revised text), or the reasoning and evidence for not changing it. Answer what was asked, not a nearby easier point. When disagreeing, acknowledge the concern, give evidence or reasoning, and say whether you clarified the text so others will not misread it. Common failures: "addressed" with no location; a change claimed but not made; tone that reads as defensive; a comment silently skipped.
elements: Every comment listed with the reviewer's numbering
A response to each comment
Location of each change in the revised text
Reasoning and evidence for each disagreement
dataNeeded: Page or line numbers of changes

sections.heading: Reviewer 2
sections.guidance: Same pattern as Reviewer 1: every comment in order with its number, the response, and the location of each change or the reasoning for none. Make sure answers do not contradict those to Reviewer 1; where the reviewers disagreed, say how you resolved it and refer to the other answer.
elements: Every comment listed with the reviewer's numbering
A response to each comment
Location of each change in the revised text
Consistency with answers to other reviewers
dataNeeded: Page or line numbers of changes

sections.heading: Reviewer 3
sections.guidance: Same pattern for a third reviewer, and add further reviewer sections the same way if there are more. NIH study sections usually have at least three assigned reviewers; in a one-page Introduction, group shared points by theme and name the reviewers who raised them instead of repeating answers.
elements: Every comment listed with the reviewer's numbering
A response and change location for each comment

sections.heading: Other Changes
sections.guidance: List changes the authors made that no reviewer asked for (updated data, new co-authors, corrected errors), so the editor and reviewers are not surprised. Keep it brief and give locations.
elements: Unrequested changes with their locations
Reason for each

rubric.criterion: Completeness: every reviewer and editor comment is answered and mapped to a change with its location or to a reasoned rebuttal.

levels.descriptor: Every comment answered in order with a specific location or a reasoned rebuttal; none merged or lost.
All answered, but a few responses lack locations.
A comment is skipped or answered only with "addressed".
Many comments unanswered or answered generically.

rubric.criterion: Disagreement: rebuttals acknowledge the concern and give evidence or reasoning, and the text is clarified where readers could misread it.

levels.descriptor: Each disagreement is respectful, evidenced and paired with a clarification where useful.
Disagreements asserted with thin reasoning.
Dismissive or defensive rebuttals with no evidence.

rubric.criterion: Accuracy: each change the response claims is present in the revised text at the stated location, and answers to different reviewers do not contradict each other.

levels.descriptor: Every claimed change is where the response says; answers are consistent across reviewers.
A location is wrong or a minor inconsistency between answers.
Claimed changes are missing from the revision, or answers contradict each other.

rubric.criterion: Form: thanks once, terse, and within the funder's or journal's length limit (one page for most NIH resubmission Introductions).

levels.descriptor: Within the limit, grouped sensibly, thanks once.
Near the limit or repetitive thanks and restatement.
Over the limit or padded.

title: Resume or CV
summary: A resume tailored to one job, or an academic curriculum vitae: contact details, a short profile, experience with measurable results, education, skills and, for a CV, publications, grants and teaching. Every fact comes from the candidate's master resume or work history.
audience: A recruiter or hiring manager scanning in under a minute, often after an applicant tracking system has parsed the text; for a CV, a search or tenure committee reading the record in the field's usual order.
tone: Concise, concrete and factual: strong verbs, results with numbers where the source has them, no first person, no clichés or self-praise.
preamble: You are a career coach tailoring the candidate's resume (or academic CV) for one target role. The candidate's master resume or work history is the source of truth: never add or change an employer, job title, date, degree, certification, skill, metric or achievement that is not in it, and keep titles and dates exactly as the master states them. Tailoring means choosing, ordering and phrasing: lead with the evidence that matches the job's required qualifications, use the posting's terms where the experience genuinely matches, keep the numbers the source gives, and trim what does not serve this role. Write bullets as action plus result, without first person. Use a single column, standard section headings, real text (no tables, images or text boxes that parsers drop) and one consistent date format. A resume is usually one to two pages depending on the field and seniority; a CV has no length limit and orders publications, grants and teaching the way the field does. Where the role asks for something the history does not show, leave it out and note it as a gap for the cover letter; never imply it. The resume is the candidate's statement: they approve every changed line.

sections.heading: Contact
sections.guidance: Name, then city and state (a full street address is not needed), phone, a professional email and one or two relevant links such as LinkedIn or a portfolio. Keep it in the document body, not a header or footer, so parsers read it.
elements: Full name
City and state
Phone and professional email
Relevant profile or portfolio link

sections.heading: Summary
sections.guidance: Two or three lines that position the candidate for this role: field and years of relevant experience, the two or three strengths the posting asks for that the history proves, and one headline result. Write in the posting's terms where they match. Common failures: an objective statement about what the candidate wants; adjectives ("passionate", "results-driven") with no evidence; claims the experience section does not back.
elements: Field and years of relevant experience
Strengths matched to the posting
One headline result

sections.heading: Experience
sections.guidance: Reverse chronological. For each role: title, employer, location and dates exactly as in the master, then three to six bullets, most relevant first. Each bullet is an action and its result, with the number the source gives (revenue, time saved, people led, volume handled). Give more space to recent and relevant roles; compress or drop old, unrelated ones. Common failures: duties listed instead of results; metrics invented or inflated; titles changed to match the posting; inconsistent date formats.
elements: Title, employer, location and dates for each role, as in the master
3-6 result-focused bullets per recent role
Most relevant evidence first
Numbers kept from the source
dataNeeded: Metrics and achievements from the master

sections.heading: Education
sections.guidance: Degree, field, institution and year (or expected year), most recent first, exactly as in the master. Add honors, a thesis title or relevant coursework only when it serves the role. Early-career candidates may place this before Experience; for a CV it usually comes first.
elements: Degree, field, institution and year for each
Honors or thesis where relevant

sections.heading: Skills
sections.guidance: Group the skills the history shows (tools, languages, methods, certifications) and put the ones the posting names first, using its spelling. Include only skills the master lists or the experience demonstrates. Common failures: long keyword lists the experience never shows; skill-level bars or graphics that parsers drop; outdated tools crowding out relevant ones.
elements: Skills grouped by kind
Posting's skills first, where the history shows them
Certifications with issuer and year

sections.heading: Publications
sections.guidance: CV variant. List publications in the citation style the field uses, grouped as the field expects (peer-reviewed articles, books, chapters, conference papers, preprints), reverse chronological, with the candidate's name highlighted. Mark status accurately (published, in press, under review). Never upgrade a submitted paper to accepted.
elements: Full citations in the field's style
Grouped by kind as the field expects
Accurate status for each

sections.heading: Grants, Fellowships and Awards
sections.guidance: CV variant, or a resume section when awards matter for the role. For each: title, funder or awarding body, the candidate's role, amount where customary, and dates, exactly as in the record.
elements: Title, funder and dates for each
Candidate's role and amount where customary

sections.heading: Teaching and Service
sections.guidance: CV variant. Courses taught (title, level, institution, terms), mentoring, and service to the department, institution and profession (committees, reviewing, editorial roles), in the order the field expects.
elements: Courses taught with level and terms
Mentoring and supervision
Professional and institutional service

rubric.criterion: Truth to the master: every employer, title, date, degree, skill and number appears in the master resume or work history.

levels.descriptor: Every fact traces to the master; titles and dates are unchanged.
A fact is reworded so that it says more than the master does.
A fact, metric or skill appears that the master does not contain.

rubric.criterion: Match to the posting: required qualifications the history supports are evident early, in the posting's terms.

levels.descriptor: Every supported required item is visible in the summary or first bullets of the relevant roles; preferred items follow.
Most supported required items are visible; one is buried.
Matching evidence exists but is hard to find or phrased in other terms.
Untailored; the resume does not address the posting.

rubric.criterion: Results: bullets state actions and outcomes with the numbers the source gives, not duties.

levels.descriptor: Most bullets show a result, quantified where the source allows.
A mix of results and duty lists.
Duty lists throughout.

rubric.criterion: Format: single column, standard headings, real text, consistent dates, length suited to the field.

levels.descriptor: Parser-friendly layout, consistent dates and a length that fits the field and seniority.
Minor format problems, such as mixed date styles or an extra page.
Tables, graphics or headers that hide content, or a length far from the field's norm.
